blocks.h: 1. What bauxite is, and why it was treated as safe

blocks.p: Bauxite is the principal ore of aluminium and one of the largest dry bulk trades in the world. For most of the history of the IMSBC Code it was listed as a Group C cargo - that is, a cargo which is neither liable to liquefy (Group A) nor possessed of a chemical hazard (Group B). The practical consequence is the important one: a Group C cargo has no transportable moisture limit, so no moisture certificate was required, no moisture limit applied, and the cargo could lawfully be loaded wet.

blocks.h: 2. The casualty that forced the reassessment

blocks.p: The reassessment was forced by casualty, and principally by one. On 2 January 2015 the 10-year-old Bahamas-flag Supramax bulk carrier Bulk Jupiter was lost with 18 of her 19 crew, carrying bauxite. The cargo had been declared as a Group C cargo, and the IMO Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers recorded that the loss may have been caused by liquefaction of the cargo. The characteristic of the casualty was its speed: the ship was lost so rapidly that there was almost no opportunity to respond.
That single loss exposed a structural gap rather than a single failure. The cargo had been carried in accordance with its schedule, and the schedule was wrong.
The research that followed established that bauxite's moisture hazard is not classic liquefaction, and the distinction is the heart of this question.

ul: Classic liquefaction - the cargo mass itself loses shear strength and behaves as a fluid. The whole body of cargo flows, and water and solids move together.

Dynamic separation - as the ship works, vibration and ship motion compact the cargo from underneath and moisture migrates upward. A liquid slurry of water and fine solids forms ABOVE the more solid material. The result is a free surface where the ship's stability calculation assumed a solid, trimmed cargo, with the loss of effective metacentric height that follows - and, if unchecked, capsize.

blocks.p: One consequence is a practical warning sign that a watchkeeper can actually use. Because the slurry lies on top and moves out of phase with the ship's roll period, the ship develops an atypical motion - a wobble - which is not the motion the loaded condition should produce. The Global Bauxite Working Group's observation was adopted by IMO in terms: an atypical motion of the ship (wobbling) may also be indicative of cargo instability, and the master should take appropriate action.
The sequence matters, because the interim measures have been overtaken and should not be quoted as current requirements.

ul: CCC.1/Circ.2, 20 October 2015 - issued within months of the loss as an interim awareness measure. It advised masters not to accept the cargo unless the moisture content was certified below an indicative limit of 10% with the particle size distribution of the Group C schedule, or the cargo was declared Group A with TML and moisture declared, or a competent authority had assessed that it did not present Group A properties.

The Global Bauxite Working Group, with competent authorities, then researched the material's behaviour and established that bauxite presents a risk caused by moisture and that some bauxite cargoes should be treated as Group A.

CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1, 20 September 2017 - supersedes the 2015 circular, whose advice it records as having been superseded by the outcome of the research. The 10% indicative limit does not survive into Rev.1 and is not a current requirement. Rev.1 annexed the finalized Test Procedure for Determining the TML for Bauxite, the new Group A schedule with the Bulk Cargo Shipping Name BAUXITE FINES, and amendments to the Group C BAUXITE schedule.
Amendment 05-19, adopted by resolution MSC.462(101), brought all three into the Code and became mandatory on 1 January 2021.

blocks.h: 5. What governs at this sitting, and which schedule applies

blocks.p: The IMSBC Code is mandatory under SOLAS chapters VI and VII, and the edition in force is amendment 07-23, mandatory since 1 January 2025. Bauxite now has two individual schedules, and everything else follows from which one the cargo falls into:

ul: BAUXITE - Group C. The coarser material. No TML applies.
BAUXITE FINES - Group A, a cargo which may undergo dynamic separation. A TML applies and the moisture content must be kept below it.

blocks.p: The separation is by particle size distribution. The Test Procedure for Determining the TML for Bauxite applies to bauxite containing both more than 30% of fine particles less than 1 mm and more than 40% of particles less than 2.5 mm - the fine, drainage-poor material that holds moisture. The TML is determined by the Modified Proctor/Fagerberg test procedure for Bauxite, taken as the critical moisture content at 80% degree of saturation where the optimum moisture content occurs at saturation of 90% or above, and at 70% where it occurs below 90%.

The governing principle for the ship is unchanged and should be stated explicitly: the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its individual schedule govern - never the commodity name. "Bauxite" on a fixture note is not a classification.

ul: Obtain the shipper's declaration required by SOLAS regulation VI/2 and section 4 of the Code, giving the BCSN, the group and the cargo's properties. Satisfy yourself that the BCSN matches what is actually being offered.

If the cargo is BAUXITE FINES or any Group A cargo, require the certificate of TML and the certificate of moisture content. Under section 4.5 the TML test must have been carried out within six months of loading, and the moisture content sampled and tested as near as practicable to loading and never more than seven days before it.
Check where and how the cargo has been stored - open stockpiles in a wet season are the single best predictor of trouble - and the loading port's recent and forecast weather.

Prepare the holds: clean and dry, bilge wells clear and tested, strainers and bilge covers in place and sealed so that fine material cannot blind the suctions, and sounding pipes clear. A bilge system that cannot be sounded or pumped is useless precisely when it matters.
Confirm the loading plan and stability, and for a bulk carrier the loading instrument and the requirements of SOLAS chapter XII, including water level detectors and alarms.
For a Group A cargo the rule is simple and absolute: the moisture content must be below the TML. If it is not, the cargo must not be loaded.
Inspect what is coming aboard. Visibly wet cargo, free water in the grab or on the conveyor, splattering, or material that flattens and glistens on the stow are all grounds to stop.
The can test is a complementary shipboard screening check, not a substitute for a TML determination. A cargo that fails it should be refused; a cargo that passes it has proved very little.
Where there has been significant rain or snow between testing and loading, check tests are required to confirm the moisture content is still below the TML.

The master is not bound by the shipper's declaration. If there is reason to doubt that the cargo is consistent with it, stop loading and require the shipper to verify the cargo's properties, seeking the advice of the competent authority of the port of loading if necessary. This is the express advice of the IMO circulars and it rests on SOLAS chapter VI.
Suspend loading in rain and close hatches; trim the cargo reasonably level to reduce the free surface available to any slurry and to limit shifting.

blocks.h: 8. Care and action on passage, and if instability develops

ul: Inspect the cargo surface daily where it is safe to do so - through hatch openings or access, without entering the space - and record what is seen. Look for free water, a slurry layer, flattening of the surface, or a change in the profile of the stow.
Sound the bilges at regular intervals, pump as necessary, and record the quantities. A rising trend is evidence, and the record is what makes it visible.
Treat atypical motion - the wobble - as a warning of cargo instability, not as a curiosity of the loaded condition.

If instability is suspected: reduce speed and alter course to ease the motion, avoid heavy weather and synchronous rolling, avoid ballasting or de-ballasting that would worsen stability, and inform owners, charterers, the flag Administration and the P&I club.
Consider seeking a port of refuge early. The Bulk Jupiter lesson is that once a slurry has formed and the ship is wobbling, the time available to act is very short.

blocks.p: The examiner's phrase is taken from the IMO circular itself, which asks that extreme care and appropriate action be taken, taking into account the provisions of relevant IMO instruments, when handling and carrying bauxite in bulk. The substance of that care is the sequence above: classify correctly, certify the moisture, refuse what is wet, watch the surface and the bilges, and act on the wobble.

The paper prints no mark allocation, and the stem contains two demands - causes and care and action - so give them roughly equal weight. The commonest failure is to spend the whole answer on a general account of liquefaction and never reach the practical care, which forfeits half the question. The second commonest is to give the care as an undifferentiated list of precautions. Answer the care limb in voyage order - before loading, during loading, on passage - because that is how it would actually be used and it is far easier to mark. Name dynamic separation early: it is the discriminating content, and an answer that never uses the term has not identified what makes bauxite different.

The printed stem is very nearly a quotation of an IMO circular. CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1 closes by inviting Member States to bring the information to the attention of the industry, "requesting that extreme care and appropriate action be taken, taking into account the provisions of relevant IMO instruments when handling and carrying Bauxite in bulk". The examiner has lifted that sentence almost word for word. Knowing this tells you what the answer is expected to contain: the casualty, the mechanism, the instruments, and the practical care - in that order.

blocks.h: The single idea that carries the answer

blocks.p: Bauxite was reclassified because of a casualty. Everything the question asks for follows from that one sentence: the causes are the reasons the old classification was wrong, and the care and action are the requirements the new classification imposes. If you open with that, the answer organises itself.

blocks.h: Dynamic separation is NOT liquefaction - and the distinction earns marks

blocks.p: This is the discriminating technical point and most candidates will blur it.

ul: In liquefaction, the cargo mass loses shear strength and the whole body flows. Water and solids move together.

In dynamic separation, the cargo compacts from underneath under vibration and motion, moisture migrates upward, and a slurry forms on top of the solid cargo. The danger is a free surface that the stability calculation never allowed for.
The behavioural tell follows from the geometry: the slurry sloshes out of phase with the roll, producing the wobble. A liquefying cargo does not do that.

blocks.h: Why a Group C classification was so dangerous

blocks.p: Not because Group C is a lax standard, but because of what it switches off. A Group C cargo has no TML, so there is no moisture certificate, no moisture limit and no basis on which a master can lawfully refuse cargo for being wet. The cargo aboard the Bulk Jupiter was carried in accordance with its schedule. The schedule was the defect. That is worth one sentence in the answer, because it shows you understand that compliance and safety are not the same thing.

ul: 2 January 2015 - Bulk Jupiter lost, 18 of 19 crew.
20 October 2015 - CCC.1/Circ.2, the interim awareness circular, with its indicative 10% moisture limit.
September 2017 - CCC 4 finalizes the test procedure and both schedules.
20 September 2017 - CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1, which supersedes the 2015 circular.
1 January 2021 - amendment 05-19, resolution MSC.462(101), becomes mandatory: BAUXITE FINES (Group A) and the revised BAUXITE (Group C).
1 January 2025 - amendment 07-23 becomes mandatory. This is the edition in force at this examination.

blocks.h: Do not quote the 10% limit as a current requirement

blocks.p: The indicative moisture limit of 10% belongs to CCC.1/Circ.2 of 2015, and it was an interim measure adopted while the research was running and before any Group A bauxite schedule existed. Rev.1 expressly supersedes that circular and records that its advice "has been superseded by the outcome of the research undertaken". Rev.1 carries no indicative moisture limit at all. Since 1 January 2021 the position is governed by the schedules and by a cargo-specific TML determined by test. Quote the 10% figure as history if you like - it shows you know the sequence - but never as the operative limit.

blocks.h: Numbers you can state, and numbers you cannot

ul: Can state: the particle-size criteria - more than 30% of particles less than 1 mm and more than 40% less than 2.5 mm; the six month TML testing interval and the seven day moisture testing interval; the saturation figures 80% and 70% in the Modified Proctor/Fagerberg procedure for bauxite.

Cannot state: a TML value for bauxite. TML is cargo-specific and determined by test for each shipment. Any general figure is wrong by construction, and offering one suggests you think TML is a property of the commodity rather than of the consignment.
Writing a generic liquefaction answer. Bauxite's mechanism is dynamic separation, and saying so is the point of the question.
Saying bauxite is a Group A cargo. BAUXITE is Group C; BAUXITE FINES is Group A. Which applies depends on particle size distribution, and the declared BCSN governs.
Quoting the 10% indicative limit as current. It is superseded.
Offering a TML figure for bauxite. TML is determined per shipment by test.
Treating the can test as a substitute for a TML certificate. It is a complementary screening check only.
Forgetting that the master may stop loading and require verification. The declaration is a starting point, not a defence.
Omitting the practical shipboard limb - daily surface inspection, bilge sounding and records, and the wobble.

blocks.p:
"The shipper hands you a Group C declaration for bauxite. Are you satisfied?" Not necessarily. Ask whether the material meets the Group C schedule's particle size distribution, how and where it has been stockpiled, and what the weather has been. If it is fine material that has been sitting in the open in the wet season, the declaration is questionable and you may stop loading and require verification.

"Your cargo passed the can test. Can you load?" The can test is a complementary screening check. Passing it does not establish that moisture content is below TML - only a certificate based on the proper test procedure does that.

"The ship has developed an odd wobble two days out. What do you do?" Treat it as evidence of cargo instability. Reduce speed and ease the motion, inspect the surface where safe, sound and record the bilges, avoid heavy weather, notify owners, charterers, flag and club, and consider a port of refuge early.

ul: Which SOLAS chapters make the IMSBC Code mandatory? Chapters VI and VII.
Name the two bauxite schedules and their groups. BAUXITE, Group C; BAUXITE FINES, Group A.
What separates them? Particle size distribution - more than 30% below 1 mm and more than 40% below 2.5 mm marks the fine material.
What is dynamic separation? Moisture migrating upward as the cargo compacts, forming a slurry with a free surface above the solid cargo.
Which casualty drove the change? Bulk Jupiter, 2 January 2015, 18 of 19 crew lost.
How long before loading must the TML and moisture tests be? TML within six months; moisture within seven days.
Which test procedure determines bauxite TML? The Modified Proctor/Fagerberg test procedure for Bauxite.
What does an atypical wobble tell you? Possible cargo instability - take action.

blocks.p: Causes then care. Causes: C-M-M - Classification wrong (1), Mechanism misunderstood (3), Moisture uncontrolled (2). Care in voyage order: D-T-R-W - Declaration and documents before loading (6), Test and refuse what is wet during loading (7), Record bilges and inspect on passage (8), Wobble means act (8).

Vibration and ship motion compact the cargo from underneath, moisture migrates upward, and a liquid slurry forms ABOVE the solid cargo - a free surface the stability calculation never allowed for. Because the slurry moves out of phase with the roll, the ship develops an atypical motion, a wobble, which IMO records as indicative of cargo instability. The response, in order. CCC.1/Circ.2, 20 October 2015 - interim, with an indicative 10% moisture limit; then Global Bauxite Working Group research; then CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1, 20 September 2017, which SUPERSEDES it (so the 10% figure is NOT current) and annexes the TML test procedure and both schedules; then amendment 05-19, resolution MSC.462(101), mandatory 1 January 2021. At this sitting the Code is mandatory under SOLAS chapters VI and VII and the edition is amendment 07-23, mandatory since 1 January 2025. Two schedules: BAUXITE - Group C; BAUXITE FINES - Group A, which may undergo dynamic separation. Separated by particle size distribution: the bauxite TML test procedure applies where there is more than 30% of particles less than 1 mm AND more than 40% less than 2.5 mm. TML is by the Modified Proctor/Fagerberg procedure for Bauxite - critical moisture at 80% saturation where OMC is at 90% saturation or above, 70% where below. The declared BCSN and its schedule govern, never the commodity name. Before loading: shipper's declaration under SOLAS VI/2; for Group A the TML certificate within six months and moisture content within seven days; check stockpile exposure and weather; holds clean and dry with bilges tested and strainers covered; loading instrument and SOLAS XII water level alarms. During loading: moisture must be below TML; reject visibly wet or splattering cargo; the can test is a screening check, never a substitute; check tests after rain or snow; the master may stop loading and require the shipper to verify, seeking the competent authority; suspend in rain; trim level. On passage: daily surface inspection where safe, sound and record bilges, watch for free water, slurry or flattening, and treat a wobble as cargo instability - reduce speed, ease the motion, avoid heavy weather, notify owners, charterers, flag and club, and consider a port of refuge early. No TML value is quotable - it is determined by test for each shipment.

quick_revision.major_trap: Writing a generic liquefaction answer. Bauxite's hazard is dynamic separation - the cargo compacts from underneath and moisture migrates upward to form a slurry above the solid material, creating a free surface - and naming and explaining that mechanism is the point of the question. The second trap is the classification. Classification and carriage requirements follow the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its current individual schedule, never the commodity name used in the question - and on that basis the Code carries two schedules, BAUXITE (Group C) and BAUXITE FINES (Group A), separated by particle size distribution. The third is temporal: the indicative moisture limit of 10% comes from CCC.1/Circ.2 of 2015, which CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1 expressly superseded in 2017; quoting it as a current requirement is wrong. The fourth is offering a TML value for bauxite - TML is determined by test for each shipment and no general figure exists.

questions.understand_first: A cargo does not become dangerous because it is reclassified; it was always dangerous, and the classification was wrong. Bauxite sat in the IMSBC Code as a Group C cargo, which meant it had no transportable moisture limit - so nobody had to certify its moisture and no master had a lawful basis to refuse it for being wet. The Bulk Jupiter was carried in full compliance with that schedule and was lost with 18 of her 19 crew. Everything that has happened since - the circulars, the research, the new Group A schedule for BAUXITE FINES - is the regulatory system correcting a classification, and the practical care the question asks about is simply what that corrected classification now requires.
questions.memory_cue: Causes first, care second. Causes: C-M-M - Classification was wrong (1-2), Moisture uncontrolled because Group C has no TML (1), Mechanism is dynamic separation not liquefaction (3). Then the response in order (4) and what governs now (5). Care in voyage order: D-T-R-W - Declaration and documents before loading (6), Test and refuse what is wet during loading (7), Record bilges and inspect the surface on passage (8), Wobble means act (8).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the bauxite question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What bauxite is and why it was treated as safe. 2 The casualty that forced the reassessment. 3 The mechanism - dynamic separation. 4 The regulatory response in sequence. 5 What governs now and which schedule applies. 6 Care before loading. 7 Care during loading. 8 Care on passage and if instability develops.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for causes and then care, so the route front-loads the mechanism and then follows the voyage in order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish dynamic separation from liquefaction.
retrieval_cards.answer: In liquefaction the cargo mass loses shear strength and the whole body flows, water and solids moving together. In dynamic separation the cargo compacts from underneath under vibration and ship motion, moisture migrates upward, and a liquid slurry of water and fine solids forms above the solid cargo - producing a free surface the stability calculation never allowed for.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating technical point of the whole question, and most candidates blur it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is bauxite a Group A cargo?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not as such. There are two schedules: BAUXITE is Group C, and BAUXITE FINES is Group A, a cargo which may undergo dynamic separation. Which applies turns on particle size distribution, and the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its individual schedule govern - never the commodity name.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying 'bauxite is Group A' is as wrong as the old position that it was always Group C.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What particle size distribution marks out the fine material, and how is its TML found?
retrieval_cards.answer: The bauxite TML test procedure applies to cargoes containing both more than 30% of fine particles less than 1 mm and more than 40% of particles less than 2.5 mm. TML is determined by the Modified Proctor/Fagerberg test procedure for Bauxite - the critical moisture content at 80% degree of saturation where the optimum moisture content occurs at 90% saturation or above, and at 70% where it occurs below 90%.
retrieval_cards.why: Fine, poorly draining material holds moisture; the criteria are the Code's way of identifying it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What was the indicative moisture limit of 10%, and can you rely on it?
retrieval_cards.answer: It came from CCC.1/Circ.2 of 20 October 2015, an interim awareness measure issued after the Bulk Jupiter loss and before any Group A bauxite schedule existed. CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1 of 20 September 2017 expressly supersedes that circular and carries no indicative limit. Since amendment 05-19 became mandatory on 1 January 2021 the position is governed by the schedules and by a cargo-specific TML determined by test.
retrieval_cards.why: Quoting a superseded interim figure as an operative limit is the temporal trap on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How recent must the TML and moisture content tests be?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under IMSBC section 4.5, the TML test must have been carried out within six months of loading, and sampling and testing for moisture content as near as practicable to the commencement of loading and never more than seven days before it. Where there has been significant rain or snow between testing and loading, check tests are required.
retrieval_cards.why: Six months and seven days - two different intervals for two different things, and the rain provision is what catches a stockpile.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are your preparations and checks before and during loading?
retrieval_cards.answer: Obtain the shipper's declaration under SOLAS VI/2 with the BCSN and group; for Group A require TML and moisture certificates within their intervals; check stockpile exposure and weather; prepare holds clean and dry with bilges tested and strainers covered. During loading, confirm moisture is below TML, reject visibly wet or splattering cargo, run check tests after rain, suspend loading in rain, and trim level.
retrieval_cards.why: The care limb is half the marks and it is answered in voyage order, not as a list of principles.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the can test let you accept the cargo?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The can test is a complementary shipboard screening check only. A cargo that fails it should be refused, but a cargo that passes it has not been shown to have a moisture content below its TML - only a certificate based on the proper test procedure does that.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating a screening check as proof is a classic way of turning a precaution into a false reassurance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The ship develops an unusual wobble two days out. What is it and what do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: It may indicate cargo instability - a free-surface slurry moving out of phase with the ship's roll period. IMO records the observation expressly. Reduce speed and alter course to ease the motion, inspect the cargo surface where safe, sound and record the bilges, avoid heavy weather and synchronous rolling, avoid ballast changes that would worsen stability, notify owners, charterers, flag and club, and consider a port of refuge early.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one warning sign a watchkeeper can actually detect, and the time available after it appears is short.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The shipper's declaration says Group C. Are you bound by it?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. If there is reason to doubt that the cargo being loaded is consistent with the declaration, the master should stop loading and have the shipper verify the cargo's properties, seeking advice from the competent authority of the loading country if necessary. That is the express advice of the IMO circulars and it rests on SOLAS chapter VI.
retrieval_cards.why: The Bulk Jupiter cargo was declared Group C and carried in accordance with its schedule. The declaration is a starting point, not a defence.

blocks.h: 1. a) What CII is, and where it sits in MARPOL

blocks.p: The Carbon Intensity Indicator is the operational half of the IMO's short-term GHG measure, imposed by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28, 'Operational carbon intensity'. It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above - the threshold of the IMO Data Collection System under regulation 27, on whose fuel data it runs. It must be distinguished from EEXI, a one-off design index applying from 400 gt: EEXI asks what the ship is capable of, CII what she actually did last year.

blocks.h: 2. How attained and required CII are set, and how a ship is rated

ul: The ship calculates an attained annual operational CII - CO2 per unit of transport work over the calendar year. For most cargo ship types this is the AER, CO2 divided by deadweight capacity multiplied by distance sailed; cruise and ro-pax types use a different metric.

The required annual operational CII is the 2019 reference line for that ship type and size reduced by a factor Z: required CII = reference value x (1 - Z/100). Z is 5% for 2023, 7% for 2024, 9% for 2025 and 11% for 2026, and was extended by resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025 to 13.625%, 16.250%, 18.875% and 21.500% for 2027 to 2030.
The attained value is verified annually and the ship rated A to E, C being the required standard, the rating recorded with the Statement of Compliance issued under the DCS.
The factors were set so that, in combination with the rest of Annex VI, shipping reduces CO2 per transport work by at least 40% by 2030 compared with 2008.

blocks.h: 3. What follows from a poor rating

blocks.p: There is no fine and no detention. The consequence is administrative: a ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for one year, must develop a corrective action plan showing how the required index of C or above will be achieved. It is incorporated in SEEMP Part III and agreed before the Statement of Compliance is issued, so a ship that ignores it cannot keep her documentation in order. Incentives to A- and B-rated ships are encouraged.

blocks.h: 4. The commercial impact on the shipping business

blocks.p: The commercial effect far exceeds the regulatory sanction, because the rating is a public, comparable letter grade on an asset:

ul: Chartering. Charterers screen tonnage on rating and some will not fix D or E ships. Because a time charterer controls speed and routing - the very things that set the rating - CII clauses are now standard, notably the BIMCO CII Operations Clause 2022. Who bears a bad rating has become a negotiated term.

Operational control shifts. Owners reserve rights over speed, hull and propeller cleaning and voyage optimisation, so slow steaming becomes contractual - with the machinery consequences of prolonged low-load running that follow.
Finance. Lenders under the Poseidon Principles report portfolio climate alignment, so rating feeds into the cost and availability of debt.
Asset value. A persistent D or E shortens commercial life, depresses second-hand values and brings forward retrofit or scrapping decisions.
Cargo owners. Shippers reporting their own scope 3 emissions demand rating data, so pressure comes from the cargo side as well as the regulatory side.

blocks.h: 5. b) The shortcomings the industry has identified

ul: It rewards capacity, not cargo. The AER denominator is deadweight capacity times distance, not cargo carried, so a ship can improve her rating by sailing further with less on board while absolute emissions rise - a genuine perverse incentive.

Waiting is punished, sailing is not. Idling at anchor adds fuel but no distance. Port congestion and 'sail fast then wait' lie outside the ship's control, and the incentive to keep moving can increase emissions.

Trade patterns are penalised structurally. Short-sea, multi-parcel chemical and product, offshore and ice-class vessels and ships with long port stays are disadvantaged by a metric built around long laden passages, however efficiently run.
Responsibility and control are split. The rating attaches to the ship and the owner's documentation, but a time charterer determines speed, route, waiting and cargo intake.
It is an efficiency ratio used as a climate instrument. Being indexed rather than absolute, improving average CII does not itself guarantee a fall in total emissions.

blocks.h: 6. The remedial measures adopted, and how far the review had got

blocks.p: The regulation anticipated this. Regulation 28.11 requires a review of the CII requirements to be completed by 1 January 2026, covering effectiveness, reinforced corrective action, enforcement, the data collection system, and revision of the Z factor and reference values.

ul: Phase 1 was completed at MEPC 83 in April 2025: implementation experience was gathered and analysed and a list of challenges and gaps identified.
Resolution MEPC.400(83), adopted 11 April 2025, amended the G3 Guidelines to set the 2027 to 2030 reduction factors, aligning them with the 2023 GHG Strategy's carbon-intensity ambition.
The SEEMP Guidelines were also amended to allow other CII metrics to be developed at future sessions - the door through which a cargo-based metric would have to come.

MEPC 83 additionally approved draft amendments to regulations 20, 25 and 28, circulated by Circular Letter No.5005 of 11 April 2025 with a view to adoption at an extraordinary session in October 2025. At this sitting that session had not met: the amendments were approved but neither adopted nor in force.
The industry's own remedies have been contractual - the BIMCO clause - and operational, through just-in-time arrival and virtual arrival schemes aimed at waiting time.

blocks.p: The honest position at this sitting is therefore this. The shortcomings had been formally acknowledged and the review was under way but not complete, with its regulation 28.11 deadline of 1 January 2026 still ahead. What had actually been adopted was an extension of the reduction factors to 2030 and an amendment permitting alternative metrics to be developed; what had been approved and was awaiting adoption was the regulation 20, 25 and 28 package. The metric itself - the source of most of the criticism - had not been changed, and the remaining stages of the review were still to come.

Limb (a) carries 10 of the 16 marks and two-thirds of candidates spend all of it on the formula. The four steps force the answer up the ladder from instrument to money, and the commercial half is where the differentiating marks are. Limb (b) is short and is best answered as mechanism then remedy, because a list of complaints without the mechanism that causes them reads as grumbling rather than analysis.

blocks.h: Why an indexed measure behaves this way

blocks.p: Any ratio can be improved by growing the denominator instead of shrinking the numerator. CII's denominator is transport work, and transport work was defined using deadweight capacity because capacity is a known, verifiable number that appears on every certificate, whereas cargo actually carried is commercially sensitive, unevenly recorded and open to manipulation. The choice was made for auditability, and the perverse incentives are the price of that choice. This is worth understanding rather than memorising, because it explains why the fix is hard: a cargo-based metric would need a trustworthy, global, verifiable source of cargo data that does not currently exist.

blocks.h: CII, EEXI, EEDI and the proposed Net-Zero Framework - keeping them apart

ul: EEDI - design index, new ships, regulation 22. What the ship was built to do.
EEXI - design index applied retrospectively to existing ships from 400 gt, regulation 23. A one-off calculation, often satisfied by engine or shaft power limitation.
CII - operational, annual, ships of 5,000 GT and above, regulation 28. What she actually did.

The Net-Zero Framework - a proposed new MARPOL Annex VI chapter, a fuel-intensity standard with a pricing mechanism. At this sitting it had been approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 and circulated for adoption at the extraordinary session MEPC/ES.2 (14 to 17 October 2025), which had not yet met. CII was in force and enforceable; the Net-Zero Framework was not adopted and not in force.

blocks.h: What the examiner means by 'remedial measures adopted'

blocks.p: This is the trap in limb (b), and it is a trap about verbs. The industry has asked for a great many things - a cargo-based metric, an exemption for waiting time, relief for short-sea trades. Almost none of that had been adopted. What had been adopted by this sitting was narrower and more procedural: the reduction factors were extended to 2030 by MEPC.400(83), Phase 1 of the review was completed, and the SEEMP Guidelines were amended so that alternative metrics could be developed later. Writing the wish-list as though it were the outcome is the commonest way to lose limb (b), and it is also simply inaccurate.

blocks.h: Approved, adopted, in force - and why September 2025 sits between two of them

blocks.p: This sitting falls in a narrow and examinable gap. MEPC 83 met from 7 to 11 April 2025, five months before the paper. It adopted resolution MEPC.400(83) - so the 2027 to 2030 reduction factors are settled law of the guidelines and belong in the answer as accomplished. In the same week it merely approved draft amendments to regulations 20, 25 and 28, and separately approved the Net-Zero Framework, circulating both by Circular Letter No.5005 with a view to adoption at the extraordinary session MEPC/ES.2 (14 to 17 October 2025). quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) What it is. The Carbon Intensity Indicator, the operational half of the short-term GHG measure, imposed by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28 on ships of 5,000 GT and above - the same threshold as the IMO DCS under regulation 27, whose fuel data it uses. Distinguish EEXI, a one-off design index from 400 gt: EEXI is what she can do, CII is what she did. How it works. Attained annual operational CII is CO2 per transport work, for most cargo ships the AER - CO2 divided by deadweight capacity times distance. Required CII is the 2019 reference line reduced by Z: required = reference x (1 - Z/100), Z being 5, 7, 9 and 11 per cent for 2023 to 2026 and, by resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025, 13.625, 16.250, 18.875 and 21.500 per cent for 2027 to 2030. Verified annually, rated A to E with C the required standard, recorded with the DCS Statement of Compliance. Consequence: no fine and no detention, but D for three consecutive years or E for one requires a corrective action plan in SEEMP Part III, agreed before the SoC issues. Commercial impact: charterers screen on rating and CII clauses are now standard (BIMCO 2022); control of speed and routing becomes a contractual issue; lenders under the Poseidon Principles price it into debt; persistent D or E depresses second-hand value and brings scrapping forward; and cargo owners want the data for their own scope 3 reporting. (b) Shortcomings: it measures capacity, not cargo, so a long ballast leg improves the rating while emissions rise; waiting at anchor is punished and sailing is not; short-sea, chemical, offshore and ice-class trades are structurally disadvantaged; responsibility sits with the owner while the time charterer controls speed, route and waiting; and it is an efficiency ratio, so a better average does not guarantee lower total emissions. Remedies adopted: regulation 28.11 required the review to be completed by 1 January 2026; Phase 1 was completed at MEPC 83 in April 2025; MEPC.400(83) extended the factors to 2030; and the SEEMP Guidelines were amended to allow other CII metrics to be developed later. A further package amending regulations 20, 25 and 28 was approved at MEPC 83 and circulated for adoption at an extraordinary session in October 2025 - which had not met when this paper was sat. Industry's own answers have been contractual and operational - the BIMCO clause, just-in-time and virtual arrival. At this sitting the metric itself was unchanged and the rest of the review was still to come.

questions.understand_first: CII is not a cap on emissions and not a trading scheme. It is an efficiency ratio - carbon per unit of transport work - turned into a public letter grade, and almost everything interesting about it follows from those two facts. Because it is a ratio, it can be improved by increasing the denominator rather than reducing emissions, which is where the shortcomings come from. Because it is a public grade attached to an asset, its real force is commercial rather than regulatory: the regulation itself imposes no fine, but a charterer, a bank and a buyer all read the letter. Keep those two ideas separate and both limbs of the question answer themselves.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the CII question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What CII is and where it sits in MARPOL. 2 How attained and required CII are set and how a ship is rated. 3 What follows from a poor rating. 4 The commercial impact. 5 The shortcomings. 6 The remedial measures adopted and how far the review had got.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Under which regulation does CII bite, to which ships, and how does that differ from EEXI?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28, operational carbon intensity, applying to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above - the same threshold as the IMO Data Collection System under regulation 27, whose fuel data it uses. EEXI is a design index under regulation 23 applying from 400 gt as a one-off calculation. EEXI is what the ship is capable of; CII is what she actually did.
retrieval_cards.why: Two thresholds and two characters. Mixing 5,000 and 400 is the commonest factual slip in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the required annual operational CII calculated, and what are the reduction factors?
retrieval_cards.answer: Required CII equals the 2019 reference line for that ship type and size multiplied by (1 - Z/100). Z is 5% for 2023, 7% for 2024, 9% for 2025 and 11% for 2026, and was extended by resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025 to 13.625%, 16.250%, 18.875% and 21.500% for 2027 to 2030.
retrieval_cards.why: A bare percentage without its year is unmarkable, and the post-2026 figures come from a specific resolution adopted five months before this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to a ship that is rated D or E?
retrieval_cards.answer: There is no fine and no detention. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year, must develop a corrective action plan showing how a rating of C or above will be achieved. It is incorporated in SEEMP Part III and must be agreed before the Statement of Compliance is issued.
retrieval_cards.why: The sanction is documentary rather than penal, and that is precisely why the commercial consequences matter more than the regulatory ones.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How can a ship improve her CII rating while emitting more CO2?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the AER denominator is deadweight capacity multiplied by distance sailed, not cargo actually carried. Sailing further, or sailing in ballast, increases the denominator and improves the rating even though absolute emissions rise. Conversely, waiting at anchor burns fuel while adding no distance and worsens the rating.
retrieval_cards.why: This single mechanism explains most of the criticism in limb (b), and stating the mechanism is worth more than listing the complaints.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What remedial measures had actually been adopted by this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Phase 1 of the regulation 28.11 review was completed at MEPC 83 in April 2025; resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025 extended the reduction factors to 2030; and the SEEMP Guidelines were amended to allow other CII metrics to be developed at future sessions. The review itself was required to be completed by 1 January 2026 and was not yet complete, and the metric that causes most of the criticism was unchanged.
retrieval_cards.why: Adopted is not the same as proposed. The industry's wish-list - a cargo-based metric, relief for waiting time - had not been adopted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the split between owner and time charterer matter to CII?
retrieval_cards.answer: The rating attaches to the ship and appears on the owner's documentation, but a time charterer determines speed, route, waiting time and cargo intake - the very variables that set the rating. That mismatch between responsibility and control is why CII clauses such as the BIMCO CII Operations Clause 2022 became standard, allocating the risk of a poor rating as a negotiated term.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the clearest example of a regulatory measure changing commercial contracts, which is what limb (a) is really asking about.

retrieval_cards.prompt: At this sitting, what had MEPC 83 adopted and what had it only approved?
retrieval_cards.answer: Adopted: resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025, extending the CII reduction factors to 2030. Approved only, and circulated by Circular Letter No.5005 for adoption at the extraordinary session MEPC/ES.2 (14 to 17 October 2025): the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI regulations 20, 25 and 28, and the IMO Net-Zero Framework. The October session had not met when this paper was sat, so neither was adopted and neither was in force.

blocks.p: Particular Average is a partial loss of ship, cargo or freight caused accidentally by a peril insured against, which is not a general average loss. It is fortuitous rather than deliberate, and it falls solely on the owner of the property damaged - there is no right of contribution from the other interests. A sea striking in a forecastle door, or seawater damage to one parcel of cargo, is particular average.

blocks.h: 2. General Average, and how it differs

blocks.p: General Average is the deliberate counterpart. Under Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules: "There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure." The loss is then shared rateably by all the interests saved - ship, cargo and freight - in proportion to their contributory values. In Indian law a general average loss is defined at section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

rows: Owner of the damaged property alone
All saved interests, rateably by contributory value

blocks.h: 3. When General Average may be declared

blocks.p: Every element of Rule A must be present:

ul: a real peril to the common adventure - apprehension alone is not enough;
the act must be extraordinary - not something the ship is already bound to do under the contract of carriage;
it must be intentional and voluntary, not accidental;
it must be reasonable;
it must be for the common safety of the property in a common maritime adventure, not for one interest alone;
there must be a saving of property - if nothing is saved there is nothing to contribute to.

blocks.p: Typical acts: jettison of cargo, voluntary stranding, water damage from firefighting, machinery damage sustained in refloating, salvage and tug costs, and port-of-refuge expenses. The shipowner, normally through the Master, declares general average. The declaration is an operational step; it does not by itself establish anyone's liability or entitlement.

An average adjuster is an independent professional appointed by the shipowner to prepare the adjustment - the statement that apportions the loss. The adjuster does not declare general average and does not decide liability. The role is to:

ul: collect GA security before cargo is released - an average bond from cargo interests and a GA guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit;
determine which sacrifices and expenditures are allowable under the applicable Rules;
ascertain the contributory values of ship, cargo and freight at the termination of the adventure;
apportion the contributions rateably and issue the adjustment;
act impartially between the interests, notwithstanding that the shipowner appoints and pays him.

blocks.p: The security step is not administrative housekeeping. The shipowner has a lien on cargo for the general average contribution, and releasing the cargo destroys that lien - which is why cargo is held until the bond and guarantee are in place, and why a large general average can delay an entire container ship's cargo for months.

The York-Antwerp Rules are not law and do not apply automatically. They are a contractual regime, effective only when incorporated into the bill of lading or charterparty - which is why those documents name the edition. YAR 2016 was adopted by the Comite Maritime International at New York in May 2016, and BIMCO agreed that its forms should refer to YAR 2016; older contracts still commonly incorporate YAR 1994 or 2004. Absent incorporation, general average falls back on the applicable national law - in India, the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

Four limbs, roughly four marks each. The commonest failure is a long, admiring essay on General Average that never reaches the average adjuster - forfeiting a quarter of the question. Answer under four headings and the marks look after themselves. The PA/GA contrast is worth a small table: it is fast to write and it demonstrates the distinction rather than asserting it.

First: who declares? The shipowner declares general average, in practice through the Master. The average adjuster does not declare it - he prepares the adjustment afterwards. Candidates routinely say the adjuster declares GA, which inverts the relationship.

Second: the York-Antwerp Rules are not law. They are a contractual code. They bind only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, and the incorporating clause names the edition. Saying so, and naming YAR 2016 as the current edition while noting that 1994 and 2004 remain in live contracts, is what separates a strong answer.

blocks.h: The right of contribution is the whole point

blocks.p: PA and GA differ in one commercially decisive respect: who pays. In particular average the loss lies where it falls. In general average it is redistributed across everyone whose property was saved. That is why the shipowner has a lien on cargo for the GA contribution, and why cargo is not released until security is in place - releasing it destroys the security.

blocks.h: Which Indian statute - and which one is NOT engaged

blocks.p: The Indian statutory reference for general average is section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Two mistakes are available here and both are common. The first is citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906: it is the model for the Indian Act but is not the operative statute in an Indian examination. The second is reaching for the Merchant Shipping Act, which does not govern general average at all - general average is a matter of marine insurance and of the contract of carriage. At this sitting the operative Indian merchant shipping statute was in any event the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; but the point is that neither Act is engaged by this question.

ul: Saying the average adjuster declares GA.
Treating the York-Antwerp Rules as an international convention.
Describing PA as a small loss and GA as a big one - the distinction is intentionality and common safety, not magnitude.
Forgetting the requirement that property must actually be saved.
Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 in an Indian examination. The Indian Act is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963; general average loss is at section 66.

blocks.p:
"The Master jettisons cargo that was already on fire and unsalvageable. Is that general average?" Probably not - Rule A requires an extraordinary sacrifice of property that was still of value and at risk; sacrificing what is already lost saves nothing.

"The engine is damaged working the ship off a strand. GA or PA?" If the stranding was accidental and the machinery damage arose in a deliberate, reasonable refloating effort for the common safety, the refloating damage is generally allowable in GA - the original grounding damage is not.

ul: Quote Rule A.
What security does the adjuster collect, and from whom? Average bond from cargo interests; GA guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit.
Which edition of the York-Antwerp Rules is current? YAR 2016, adopted by the CMI in May 2016.
Where is general average loss defined in Indian law? Section 66, Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Why is cargo not released before security is posted? Because release destroys the shipowner's lien for the contribution.
Give a real example. The 2018 Maersk Honam cargo-hold fire, where GA was declared and cargo interests had to post substantial security before release.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Particular Average is a partial loss of ship, cargo or freight caused accidentally by a peril insured against, which is not a general average loss. It is fortuitous, and it falls solely on the owner of the property damaged - no contribution from anyone else. General Average is the deliberate counterpart. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules: there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure. The loss is then shared rateably by all saved interests - ship, cargo and freight - in proportion to contributory values. In Indian law, section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Every Rule A element must be present: a real peril (apprehension is not enough); an extraordinary act, not one the ship was already bound to perform; intentional and voluntary; reasonable; for the common safety, not one interest alone; and property must actually be saved. Typical acts - jettison, voluntary stranding, firefighting water damage, refloating machinery damage, salvage and tug costs, port-of-refuge expenses. The shipowner declares GA, normally through the Master; the declaration settles nobody's liability. The average adjuster is an independent professional appointed by the shipowner to prepare the adjustment. He does NOT declare GA. He secures the average bond from cargo interests and the GA guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit; allows or disallows claimed sacrifices; ascertains contributory values at the termination of the adventure; apportions rateably; and acts impartially though the shipowner pays him. Security matters because the shipowner has a lien on cargo for the contribution and release destroys it. Finally, the Rules are not law - they are contractual, effective only as incorporated by the bill of lading or charterparty, which names the edition. YAR 2016 was adopted by the CMI at New York in May 2016 and BIMCO forms refer to it; YAR 1994 and 2004 remain in live contracts. Absent incorporation, national law applies.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: York-Antwerp Rules Rule A - extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure intentionally and reasonably made for the common safety. Contractual, not law; incorporated by the bill of lading or charterparty. Indian statutory counterpart: Marine Insurance Act 1963 section 66.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the average adjuster declares GA - the shipowner does, normally through the Master; the adjuster prepares the adjustment afterwards. The second trap is treating the York-Antwerp Rules as an international convention rather than a contractual code that binds only when incorporated. A third, specific to an Indian paper, is reaching for the wrong statute: general average is Marine Insurance Act, 1963 section 66, not the UK Act of 1906 and not the Merchant Shipping Act, which does not govern general average at all.

questions.understand_first: General Average is not compensation for damage. It is the sharing out of a loss that somebody chose to suffer, on purpose, to save the whole venture - ship, cargo and freight together. Because everybody benefited from that choice, everybody contributes. Particular Average is the opposite: accidental damage, which lies where it falls.
questions.memory_cue: Two definitions then two roles. PA (1) is accidental and borne alone; GA (2) is deliberate and shared. Test GA at step 3 with E-I-R-C-S: Extraordinary, Intentional, Reasonable, Common safety, Saved - miss one and it is not general average. The adjuster at step 4 is three verbs: secure, allow, apportion - and he does not declare. Close at step 5 with contract, not convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define Particular Average.
retrieval_cards.answer: A partial loss of ship, cargo or freight caused accidentally by a peril insured against, which is not a general average loss. It falls solely on the interest damaged.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole contrast with GA hangs on two words: accidental, and alone.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define General Average.
retrieval_cards.answer: An extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure, intentionally and reasonably made in time of peril for the common safety, to preserve the property in the common maritime adventure. Contribution is shared rateably by all saved interests in proportion to their contributory values.
retrieval_cards.why: Quoting Rule A's structure rather than paraphrasing it is what earns the definition mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The single sharpest distinction between PA and GA?
retrieval_cards.answer: PA is accidental and borne alone. GA is deliberate and shared.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction is intentionality and common safety, not the size of the loss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must be present before General Average can be declared?
retrieval_cards.answer: All the Rule A elements: a real peril, not mere apprehension; a deliberate and voluntary act; an extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure, not something the ship was already bound to do; reasonableness; the common safety of the adventure rather than one interest; and an actual saving of property.
retrieval_cards.why: Six elements, and the examiner is checking whether you know that all of them must be satisfied.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Do the York-Antwerp Rules apply automatically?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. They are not law. They apply only when incorporated into the bill of lading or charterparty, which is why those documents name the edition. YAR 2016 was adopted by the CMI at New York in May 2016 and BIMCO forms refer to it, but YAR 1994 and 2004 remain in live contracts. Absent incorporation, national law applies.
retrieval_cards.why: Calling the Rules a convention is the fastest way to show you have not understood how they bind.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the average adjuster declare general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The shipowner declares it, normally through the Master. The adjuster secures the bond and guarantee, allows or disallows claims, ascertains contributory values and apportions contribution - independently and impartially, though the shipowner appoints and pays him.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying the adjuster declares GA inverts the relationship and is a frequent, costly slip.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statutory provision covers general average loss, and which statute is NOT engaged?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. The UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 is its model but is not the operative statute in an Indian examination, and the Merchant Shipping Act does not govern general average at all.
retrieval_cards.why: Two wrong statutes are readily available here, and naming the right one precisely is a cheap mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is cargo not released before general average security is posted?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the shipowner has a lien on cargo for the general average contribution, and releasing the cargo destroys the lien. The adjuster therefore collects an average bond from cargo interests and a GA guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit, before release.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why a major GA declaration can hold up an entire ship's cargo for months - the commercial consequence the examiner is looking for.

blocks.p: A maritime lien is a privileged claim against the vessel herself rather than against any person. It is not created by agreement and it is not registered: it attaches to the ship by operation of law at the moment the claim arises, and it does so without notice to anyone. Until it is enforced it is inchoate - a right in the ship that lies dormant; it is crystallised by arrest and realised by forced sale. Its practical significance is its rank: a maritime lien takes priority over a registered mortgage, even one registered earlier and for a far larger sum.
That combination - secret, unregistered, automatic and senior - is what distinguishes it from an ordinary possessory lien, which depends on holding the goods and is lost when possession is given up.

blocks.h: 2. How the lien travels with the property

blocks.p: This is the defining characteristic, and the Convention states it in one sentence. Article 8: the maritime liens follow the vessel, notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag.

ul: The lien is attached to the res - the ship - and not to the owner, so selling the ship does not shed it.

It binds a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. A buyer may acquire a ship with unpaid crew wages or a salvage award still charged against her and have no means of discovering it from any register. This is why it is called a secret lien and why prudent buyers take indemnities and searches.
Reflagging and re-registration make no difference: the lien travels with the hull, not with the certificate.
It is defeated in only two ways - by a forced sale complying with article 12, which sweeps the ship clean of liens and encumbrances, or by lapse of time under article 9.

blocks.p: Under article 9 the article 4 liens are extinguished after one year unless, before then, the vessel has been arrested or seized and that arrest or seizure leads to a forced sale. Time runs from the claimant's discharge from the vessel for wage claims and from the moment the claim arises for the others, and it runs continuously, without suspension or interruption.

ul: An action in personam is brought against a person - the owner, charterer, manager or operator. The claimant must find that person, establish jurisdiction over them, and then enforce against whatever assets they have. If the defendant is a single-ship company with no other assets, a judgment in personam may be worth nothing.

An action in rem is brought against the ship herself, which is named as defendant. The court's jurisdiction is founded on the presence of the res within the jurisdiction, and the ship may be arrested.

blocks.p: The connection between the two limbs of this question is the point the examiner is looking for: the maritime lien is what gives the claimant a right in rem against the ship. Because the lien attaches to the vessel and follows her, the claimant can proceed against the vessel wherever she is found and whoever now owns her.

Arrest is not usually an end in itself. It is a coercive step: it either compels the provision of security - a P&I club letter of undertaking or a bank guarantee - so that the ship may trade on, or, if no security is forthcoming, it produces a fund through forced sale out of which the claims are paid. The two forms of action are not alternatives and may be pursued together.

blocks.h: 4. Which convention deals with maritime liens

blocks.p: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993 and in force from 5 September 2004. It is the successor to the earlier Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967 on the same subject, neither of which achieved wide acceptance. Its stated purpose is to improve the conditions for ship financing and the development of national merchant fleets - which explains its structure: it protects mortgagees by making mortgages recognisable and enforceable across States, and it does so by defining exhaustively the small class of claims that outrank them.
Article 4(1) secures five claims, against the owner, demise charterer, manager or operator, by a maritime lien on the vessel:

ul: (a) claims for wages and other sums due to the master, officers and other members of the vessel's complement in respect of their employment on the vessel, including costs of repatriation and social insurance contributions payable on their behalf;
(b) claims in respect of loss of life or personal injury, whether on land or on water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel;
(c) claims for reward for the salvage of the vessel;
(d) claims for port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues;
(e) claims based on tort arising out of physical loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than loss of or damage to cargo, containers and passengers' effects carried on the vessel.

blocks.p: Article 4(2) removes two categories from limbs (b) and (e): damage from the carriage of oil or other hazardous or noxious substances for which compensation is payable under regimes providing strict liability and compulsory insurance, and damage from the radioactive properties of nuclear fuel, products or waste. The reasoning is that those claimants already have a dedicated fund, and there is no need to give them a lien as well.

Note what is not a maritime lien: cargo claims, and the claims of necessaries men - bunker suppliers, repairers and agents. They may be maritime claims founding an action in rem, but they carry no lien under article 4.

blocks.h: 6. How the liens rank among themselves - article 5

ul: The article 4 liens take priority over registered mortgages, "hypotheques" and charges, and no other claim takes priority over either, subject to article 12(3) and (4).
They rank in the order listed in article 4 - so wages before personal injury, before salvage, before dues, before tort.

But salvage liens jump the queue: a lien securing a claim for salvage reward takes priority over all other maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed. The logic is obvious - the salvor preserved the very fund the others are claiming against.
Liens within each of (a), (b), (d) and (e) rank pari passu among themselves.
Salvage liens rank in the inverse order of time in which the claims accrued - the later salvage ranks first - each claim being deemed to accrue on the date the salvage operation terminated.

blocks.h: 7. The order of settlement after forced sale - article 12

blocks.p: A forced sale in a State Party sweeps the vessel clean: all registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges, except those assumed by the purchaser with the holders' consent, and all liens and other encumbrances of whatsoever nature, cease to attach to the vessel, provided the ship was within that State's jurisdiction and the sale complied with its law and with articles 11 and 12. The proceeds are then distributed in this order:

ul: 1. The costs and expenses of the arrest or seizure and of the subsequent sale, paid first out of the proceeds. These expressly include the costs of upkeep of the vessel and the crew, and the wages and other sums under article 4(1)(a) incurred from the time of the arrest or seizure.

2. Wreck-removal costs, where a State Party has so provided. Article 12(3) permits a State to provide that, where a stranded or sunken vessel has been removed by a public authority in the interest of safe navigation or protection of the marine environment, those removal costs are paid before all other claims secured by a maritime lien. This is optional, not automatic.
3. The article 4 maritime liens, in their article 5 order and subject to the salvage rules.

4. The right of retention of a shipbuilder or shiprepairer under article 7. Article 12(4) requires him to surrender possession to the purchaser, but entitles him to be satisfied out of the proceeds after the article 4 lienholders.
5. Registered mortgages, "hypotheques" and charges complying with article 1.
6. Other maritime liens granted under national law under article 6, which rank after both the article 4 liens and the registered mortgages.
7. The residue, if any, to the owner, and States Parties must ensure the proceeds are actually available and freely transferable.

blocks.p: The purchaser is then entitled to a certificate that the vessel is sold free of encumbrances, on production of which the registrar must delete the registered mortgages and charges and either register the vessel in the purchaser's name or issue a certificate of deregistration.

blocks.h: 8. The Indian statutory position, kept separate

blocks.p: In India the subject is governed domestically by the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 (No. 22 of 2017, assented 9 August 2017), which consolidated admiralty jurisdiction and vested it in the High Courts. Its scheme closely follows the Convention, and the differences are worth knowing:

ul: Section 9(1) lists the same five maritime liens in the same order, with two widenings: limb (c) covers salvage including special compensation, and limb (d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel.

Section 9(2) reproduces the travelling rule - the lien continues notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag - and the one-year extinction, but with a proviso giving TWO years for wage claims under limb (a), running from the date the wage, repatriation cost or social insurance contribution fell due. That is more generous to seafarers than the Convention.

Section 10 sets the order of priority of maritime claims in an admiralty proceeding as: (a) claims where there is a maritime lien; (b) registered mortgages and charges of the same nature; (c) all other claims - with claims in a single category ranking equally, and salvage claims in inverse order of time.

blocks.p: (The stem asks about the convention, and the answer above is given at convention level. The Indian Act is set out separately because it is the law an Indian court would apply, and it should not be conflated with the Convention.)

The stem contains five separate demands in sixteen marks - define the lien, explain how it travels, explain in rem and in personam, name the convention, and give the order of settlement. That is roughly three marks each, so none of them deserves an essay and none may be skipped. The two that candidates most often lose are the last: they name the convention vaguely, or give a half-remembered priority list. The order of settlement is the single most concrete thing in the question and it is the easiest to prepare, so it should be written out as a numbered list, not narrated.

blocks.h: The idea that links the whole question

blocks.p: The lien and the action in rem are two halves of one mechanism. The maritime lien attaches to the ship rather than to a person; that is precisely what allows the claimant to sue the ship rather than a person. If you state that link explicitly - the lien is what gives the right in rem - the middle three demands of the question join up instead of reading as three unrelated definitions.

blocks.h: Why the lien is called secret, and why that matters commercially

blocks.p: There is no register of maritime liens. A buyer inspecting the ship's registry sees mortgages and charges but cannot see unpaid crew wages, an outstanding salvage award or a personal injury claim - and under article 8 all of those follow the vessel through a sale, a change of registry and a change of flag. So a purchaser can take delivery of a ship already encumbered by claims ranking ahead of the mortgage financing the purchase. This is why sale contracts carry indemnities and why a forced sale under article 12 is commercially valuable: it is the one transaction that delivers a genuinely clean ship, which is exactly why an arresting creditor's remedy has teeth.

blocks.h: The two salvage rules - state both

blocks.p: Salvage is the exception to almost every ranking rule in the Convention and both exceptions are examinable.

ul: Salvage jumps ahead of earlier liens. A salvage lien takes priority over all maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed. The salvor preserved the fund everyone else is claiming against, so he is paid first out of it.

Salvage liens rank in inverse order of time. Where there is more than one salvage, the later ranks ahead of the earlier - each claim accruing on the date its salvage operation terminated. Every other category ranks pari passu.

blocks.h: What is NOT a maritime lien

blocks.p: A quick way to show command of article 4 is to say what it leaves out. Cargo claims are not secured by a maritime lien - article 4(1)(e) expressly excludes loss of or damage to cargo, containers and passengers' effects. Nor are the claims of necessaries men - bunker suppliers, repairers, agents and chandlers. These may still be maritime claims supporting an action in rem and an arrest, but they carry no lien and therefore rank behind registered mortgages. The distinction between a maritime claim and a maritime lien is exactly what the priority list is about.

blocks.h: The Indian dimension - and the statement to avoid

blocks.p: The examiner asks about the convention, so answer at convention level. The Indian statute is the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, and giving it separately is a strength: its section 9 reproduces the five liens and their order, and its section 10 gives the three-tier priority - liens, then registered mortgages, then all other claims.

Two genuine Indian divergences are worth knowing. Section 9(1)(c) covers salvage including special compensation, and section 9(1)(d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel. Most importantly, section 9(2) gives seafarers two years for wage claims where the Convention gives one - more generous than the Convention.

What to avoid: do not assert whether or not India is a party to the 1993 Convention. It is not necessary to answer any part of this question, and a confident statement either way is a risk for no reward. Say what the Convention provides, say what the Indian Act provides, and let the two stand side by side.

ul: Confusing a maritime claim with a maritime lien. Every lien is a claim; very few claims are liens.
Saying a maritime lien is lost on sale of the ship. It is not - article 8 is the whole point of the question's second limb.
Treating in rem and in personam as alternatives. They may be pursued together.
Putting mortgages ahead of maritime liens. Article 5 puts the liens first, which is the commercially surprising and therefore examinable point.
Forgetting that arrest and sale costs and post-arrest crew wages are paid before everything, including the liens.
Omitting the salvage inverse-order rule, or applying inverse order to all categories rather than only to salvage.
Giving a mortgage a rank ahead of the shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention. Article 12(4) puts retention after the article 4 liens but the Convention leaves mortgages behind both.

blocks.p:
"You buy a ship with a clean registry search. Can you still be caught?" Yes. Maritime liens are unregistered and follow the vessel through a change of ownership, registration and flag. Only a forced sale under article 12, or the lapse of time under article 9, clears them.

"Crew wages or the bank - who is paid first?" Crew. Article 4(1)(a) is the first maritime lien and article 5(1) puts all article 4 liens ahead of registered mortgages. And the wages incurred after arrest are paid even before that, as part of the article 12(2) costs.

"Two salvage services, one in January and one in June. Who ranks first?" June - salvage liens rank in inverse order of time.

"Is a bunker supplier's claim a maritime lien under the Convention?" No. It may be a maritime claim founding an action in rem, but article 4 does not secure it, so it ranks behind registered mortgages.

ul: Define a maritime lien in one sentence. A privileged claim attaching to the vessel by operation of law, without registration or notice, which follows her through changes of ownership, registration and flag.
Which convention, adopted where and when? The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004.

List the five maritime liens in order. Wages; loss of life or personal injury; salvage; port, canal and waterway dues and pilotage; tort for physical loss or damage other than to cargo, containers and passengers' effects.
How long does a maritime lien last? One year under article 9, unless arrest or seizure leading to forced sale intervenes - and two years for wage claims under the Indian Act.
What is paid first out of a forced sale? The costs of arrest, seizure and sale, including upkeep of ship and crew and post-arrest wages.
Where do mortgages rank? After the article 4 maritime liens and after a shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention.
Which Indian statute governs? The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - section 9 for liens, section 10 for priority.

For the settlement order at step 7, work outward from the court: COSTS first, LIENS next, then the YARD, then the BANK, then the REST, then the OWNER. For the two salvage rules, salvage jumps forward, and later salvage beats earlier.

quick_revision.recall_15s: What it is. A maritime lien is a privileged claim against the vessel herself, attaching by operation of law the moment the claim arises - no agreement, no registration, no notice. It is inchoate until enforced, crystallised by arrest and realised by forced sale, and it outranks a registered mortgage however early or large. How it travels. Article 8 - the liens follow the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag. It binds a bona fide purchaser without notice, which is why it is a secret lien. It dies only by forced sale under article 12 or by lapse of time under article 9 - one year, unless arrest or seizure leading to forced sale intervenes; time runs from discharge for wages and from accrual for the rest, continuously. In rem and in personam. In personam is against a person - useless against a single-ship company with no assets. In rem is against the ship as defendant, founded on her presence in the jurisdiction, enforced by arrest. The lien is what gives the right in rem. Arrest is coercive - it compels security (club LOU or bank guarantee) or produces a fund by sale. The two may run together. The convention. The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004, successor to the Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967. Article 4 secures five claims: (a) crew wages, repatriation costs and social insurance contributions; (b) loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with operation; (c) salvage reward; (d) port, canal and waterway dues and pilotage; (e) tort for physical loss or damage, excluding cargo, containers and passengers' effects. Article 4(2) excludes oil/HNS damage compensable under strict-liability regimes, and nuclear. NOT liens: cargo claims and necessaries men - bunkers, repairs, agency. Article 5 ranking: liens beat registered mortgages; they rank in the order listed; salvage jumps ahead of all liens attached before the salvage; (a), (b), (d), (e) rank pari passu; salvage ranks in INVERSE order of time. Article 12 order of settlement after forced sale: 1 costs of arrest, seizure and sale, including upkeep of ship and crew and post-arrest wages; 2 optionally wreck-removal costs where national law so provides; 3 the article 4 liens in their order; 4 the shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention; 5 registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges; 6 national liens under article 6; 7 residue to the owner. The sale sweeps the ship clean and the registrar must delete the encumbrances. quick_revision.major_trap: Confusing a maritime claim with a maritime lien. Bunker suppliers, repairers and agents have maritime claims which will found an action in rem and an arrest, but they are not secured by a maritime lien under article 4, so they rank behind registered mortgages - the opposite of where candidates usually put them.
