The second trap is ranking mortgages ahead of liens: article 5 does the reverse, and that inversion is the commercially surprising point the question is testing. The third is forgetting that the costs of arrest, seizure and sale - including post-arrest crew wages and upkeep - are paid before even the maritime liens. The fourth is applying the inverse order of time rule to every category; it applies only to salvage.

questions.understand_first: Ordinary law says that if you are owed money you sue the person who owes it. Shipping cannot work that way: the debtor may be a single-ship company in a jurisdiction you will never reach, and the only asset is a ship that will sail tomorrow. So maritime law does something unusual - it lets a small class of claims attach to the SHIP itself, silently and automatically, and follow her wherever she goes and whoever buys her. That is a maritime lien, and the action in rem is simply the procedure for enforcing it: you sue the ship. Everything else in this question - the priority list, the arrest, the forced sale - is the machinery for turning a ship into money and then deciding who gets paid out of it, in what order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the maritime lien question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a maritime lien is. 2 How it travels with the property. 3 In rem and in personam. 4 Which convention. 5 What article 4 secures. 6 How the liens rank among themselves. 7 The order of settlement after forced sale. 8 The Indian statutory position, separately.
retrieval_cards.why: Five demands in sixteen marks, so about three marks each. None deserves an essay and none may be skipped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a maritime lien.
retrieval_cards.answer: A privileged claim against the vessel herself, attaching to her by operation of law at the moment the claim arises, without agreement, registration or notice. It is inchoate until enforced, crystallised by arrest and realised by forced sale, and it ranks ahead of registered mortgages.
retrieval_cards.why: Secret, unregistered, automatic and senior - those four words distinguish it from every ordinary lien.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a maritime lien travel with the property, and how is it ever lost?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 8 of the 1993 Convention: the maritime liens follow the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag - so they bind even a bona fide purchaser without notice. They are lost only by a forced sale complying with article 12, which sweeps the ship clean, or by lapse of time under article 9 - one year, unless arrest or seizure leading to a forced sale intervenes.
retrieval_cards.why: The travelling rule is the second demand of the stem and the Convention answers it in a single sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish an action in rem from an action in personam, and say how the lien connects them.
retrieval_cards.answer: In personam is against a person - the owner, charterer, manager or operator - and is worth only what that person's assets are worth. In rem is against the ship herself as defendant, founded on her presence within the jurisdiction and enforced by arrest. The maritime lien is what gives the claimant the right in rem, because it attaches to the vessel and follows her. The two may be pursued together.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the link turns three separate definitions into one mechanism, which is what the examiner is looking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the convention and list the five claims it secures by a maritime lien.
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993 - Geneva, 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004. Article 4: (a) crew wages, repatriation and social insurance; (b) loss of life or personal injury; (c) salvage reward; (d) port, canal and waterway dues and pilotage; (e) tort for physical loss or damage, other than to cargo, containers and passengers' effects.
retrieval_cards.why: W-P-S-D-T. The order is the ranking order too, so learning the list once does two jobs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the order of settlement of claims after a forced sale under the 1993 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Costs and expenses of arrest or seizure and of the sale, including upkeep of vessel and crew and article 4(1)(a) wages incurred from the time of arrest. 2 Optionally, wreck-removal costs where the State has so provided under article 12(3). 3 The article 4 maritime liens in their article 5 order. 4 A shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention under article 12(4). 5 Registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges. 6 Other national maritime liens under article 6. 7 The residue to the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the most concrete thing in the question and the easiest to prepare. Write it as a numbered list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two salvage services, January and June. Which lien ranks first, and why does salvage rank oddly at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: June. Salvage liens rank in the inverse order of time in which the claims accrued, each accruing when its salvage operation terminated. Salvage also takes priority over all other maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed, because the salvor preserved the very fund the other claimants are claiming against.
retrieval_cards.why: Two separate salvage rules, and inverse order applies only to salvage - not to the other categories, which rank pari passu.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a bunker supplier's claim a maritime lien under the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Bunker suppliers, repairers, agents and other necessaries men have maritime claims which may found an action in rem and support an arrest, but article 4 does not secure them by a maritime lien, so they rank behind registered mortgages. Cargo claims are excluded in terms by article 4(1)(e).
retrieval_cards.why: Every lien is a claim; very few claims are liens. Confusing the two is the commonest error in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Indian Admiralty Act 2017 differ from the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 9(1) lists the same five liens in the same order, but limb (c) covers salvage including special compensation and limb (d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel. Section 9(2) reproduces the travelling rule and the one-year extinction but adds a proviso giving two years for wage claims - more generous to seafarers than the Convention. Section 10 gives a three-tier priority: maritime liens, then registered mortgages and charges, then all other claims, with equal ranking within a category and salvage in inverse order of time.
retrieval_cards.why: It is an Indian examination, so the domestic statute earns marks - but keep it separate from the Convention rather than merging the two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Crew wages or the mortgagee bank - who is paid first out of a forced sale?
retrieval_cards.answer: The crew. Article 5(1) puts all article 4 maritime liens ahead of registered mortgages, and wages are the first lien in the article 4 list. Wages and upkeep incurred after the arrest rank even higher, as part of the article 12(2) costs paid first out of the proceeds.
retrieval_cards.why: It is commercially counter-intuitive that an unregistered claim beats a registered mortgage, which is exactly why it is examined.

Article 1.5 defines HNS as 'any substances, materials and articles carried on board a ship as cargo' in seven listed categories (i) to (vii), plus article 1.5(b) residues from previous bulk carriage of (a)(i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii). Article 1.5bis defines bulk HNS as (a)(i)-(iii), (v)-(vii) and (b); article 1.5ter defines packaged HNS as (a)(iv).

PRIMARY - HNS article 1.6: 'Damage' means (a) loss of life or personal injury on board or outside the ship caused by those substances; (b) loss of or damage to property outside the ship; (c) loss or damage by contamination of the environment, 'provided that compensation for impairment of the environment other than loss of profit from such impairment shall be limited to costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken'; and (d) the costs of preventive measures and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures. The article closes by providing for the case where it is not reasonably possible to separate HNS damage from damage caused by other factors.

PRIMARY - HNS article 4: 4.1 applies to claims 'other than claims arising out of any contract for the carriage of goods and passengers'; 4.2 disapplies the Convention where incompatible with workers' compensation or social security schemes; 4.3(a) excludes 'pollution damage as defined in the International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage, 1969, as amended, whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention'; 4.3(b) excludes damage caused by radioactive material of class 7 in the IMDG Code or the IMSBC Code; 4.4 excludes warships and State non-commercial ships.

PRIMARY - HNS articles 7, 9, 12, 14 and 37. Article 7.1 imposes strict liability on the owner, with the defences in 7.2(a)-(d) including failure of the shipper to furnish information on the hazardous nature of the substances; article 7.5 channels claims away from crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator and salvor. Article 9.1(a) limits bulk-HNS liability to 10 million units of account up to 2,000 units of tonnage, rising by 1,500 and then 360 units per ton, capped at 100 million units of account; article 9.1(b) sets the packaged-HNS (or mixed, or indeterminate) figures at 11.5 million rising by 1,725 and 414, capped at 115 million units of account. Article 12 requires the owner of a ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS to maintain insurance in the sums fixed by article 9.1, evidenced by a compulsory insurance certificate in the Annex I model form, carried on board, mutually recognised between States Parties, and subject to direct action against the insurer under 12.8. Article 14.5(a) caps the HNS Fund so that the total of Fund compensation and any amount paid under chapter II shall not exceed 250 million units of account. Article 37 extinguishes rights after three years from knowledge, and in no case later than ten years from the incident.

PRIMARY - 1992 Civil Liability Convention, consolidated text (IOPC Funds, Texts of the Conventions), read for the limb (c) boundary. Article I.5: 'Oil' means any persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil such as crude oil, fuel oil, heavy diesel oil and lubricating oil, whether carried on board a ship as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship. Article I.6(a): 'Pollution damage' means loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of oil. Article I.1 treats a combination carrier as a 'ship' only when actually carrying oil in bulk as cargo and on a following voyage unless it is proved she retains no residues. Article VII.1 requires insurance of a ship carrying more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo.

PRIMARY - 2001 Bunkers Convention, official published treaty text, read for the same boundary. Article 1.5: 'Bunker oil' means any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil. Article 1.9(a): 'Pollution damage' is loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination from bunker oil. Article 4.1: 'This Convention shall not apply to pollution damage as defined in the Civil Liability Convention, whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention.' Article 7.1 requires insurance for a registered owner of a ship of gross tonnage greater than 1000.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention, and its status at this sitting

blocks.p: The instrument is the International Convention on Liability and Compensation for Damage in Connection with the Carriage of Hazardous and Noxious Substances by Sea - the 1996 Convention as amended by the 2010 Protocol, which by article 18 of that Protocol are 'read and interpreted together as one single instrument' and cited as the 2010 HNS Convention. It does for hazardous and noxious cargoes what the CLC and Fund Conventions do for persistent oil: strict liability on the owner, backed by compulsory insurance and a second tier financed by cargo interests. As the question states, it had not yet entered into force and was expected to do so shortly.

blocks.h: 2. a) The substances covered - the seven categories of article 1.5

blocks.p: The Convention does not list commodities. Article 1.5(a) defines HNS as any substances, materials and articles carried on board a ship as cargo falling within seven categories, each defined by reference to an existing IMO instrument - so the HNS list updates automatically as those instruments are amended:

ul: (i) Oils carried in bulk, as defined in regulation 1 of MARPOL Annex I - crude oil, fuel oil, heavy diesel, lubricating oil.

(ii) Noxious liquid substances carried in bulk, as defined in regulation 1.10 of MARPOL Annex II, together with substances provisionally categorised in pollution category X, Y or Z under regulation 6.3 - for example vegetable oils and phosphoric acid.

(iii) Dangerous liquid substances carried in bulk listed in chapter 17 of the IBC Code, and products for which preliminary carriage conditions have been prescribed under paragraph 1.1.6 - benzene, styrene monomer, methanol, sulphuric acid.
(iv) Dangerous, hazardous and harmful substances, materials and articles in packaged form covered by the IMDG Code - drummed and containerised chemicals, corrosives, explosives, flammable solids.
(v) Liquefied gases listed in chapter 19 of the IGC Code, and products prescribed under paragraph 1.1.6 - LNG, LPG, ammonia, ethylene, vinyl chloride monomer.
(vi) Liquid substances carried in bulk with a flashpoint not exceeding 60°C measured by closed-cup test - gasoline, naphtha, and similar light products.

(vii) Solid bulk materials possessing chemical hazards covered by the IMSBC Code, to the extent that they are also subject to the IMDG Code in effect in 1996 when carried in packaged form - ammonium nitrate and ammonium nitrate based fertilizers, seed cake.

blocks.p: Article 1.5(b) extends the definition to residues from the previous carriage in bulk of substances in (a)(i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii), so a tank that has been discharged but not cleaned still carries HNS for the purposes of the Convention.

blocks.h: 3. a) Bulk HNS and packaged HNS - why the split matters

blocks.p: Article 1.5bis defines bulk HNS as categories (i) to (iii) and (v) to (vii) together with residues; article 1.5ter defines packaged HNS as category (iv) alone. The distinction is not academic: it sets the owner's limit of liability under article 9 and, in the second tier, packaged cargo does not contribute to the Fund in the way bulk cargo does.

blocks.h: 4. b) The heads of damage - article 1.6

blocks.p: 'Damage' is defined in article 1.6 and is significantly wider than pollution. It comprises four heads:

ul: (a) Loss of life or personal injury, whether on board or outside the ship carrying the substances, caused by those substances.
(b) Loss of or damage to property outside the ship caused by those substances.

(c) Loss or damage by contamination of the environment - with the standard limitation that compensation for impairment of the environment, other than loss of profit from that impairment, is confined to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken.
(d) The costs of preventive measures, and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

blocks.p: Two consequences follow, and they are where the marks are. First, because heads (a) and (b) are not qualified by the word contamination, the Convention reaches fire, explosion, toxicity and reactivity damage - the characteristic ways a chemical or gas cargo actually causes harm - and not merely spillage. That is the single most important structural difference between HNS and the oil-pollution conventions, which are contamination regimes. Secondly, economic loss consequential on contamination, of the kind suffered by fishing, mariculture and tourism interests, is recoverable through head (c). Where damage caused by the HNS cannot reasonably be separated from damage caused by other factors, the article deems the whole of it to be HNS damage.

blocks.h: 5. b) What is excluded, and the mechanism that excludes it

ul: CLC pollution damage. By article 4.3(a) the Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is actually payable under it - so the exclusion bites on the definition, not on the outcome of a claim.
Radioactive material of class 7 in the IMDG or IMSBC Codes, by article 4.3(b).
Claims arising out of a contract for the carriage of goods or passengers, by article 4.1 - cargo claims remain a matter for the bill of lading and the Hague-Visby or Hamburg regime.
Workers' compensation and social security, to the extent of incompatibility, by article 4.2; and warships and State non-commercial ships, by article 4.4.

blocks.p: One exclusion is commonly stated and is not in the text. Bunker oil is not excluded by any article of this Convention; the word does not appear in it. Bunkers fall outside because article 1.5(a) covers only substances carried as cargo. A ship's own fuel is not cargo, so it is never HNS in the first place - which is precisely why a separate Bunkers Convention was needed.

blocks.h: 6. c) Why an oil products tanker needs certificates under all three conventions

blocks.p: Because the three regimes are mutually exclusive but jointly incomplete, and which of them applies to this ship changes with the parcel she happens to be carrying. Two variables do the work: what the substance is, and how the damage arises.

ul: CLC 92 covers only persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil (article I.5) and only damage by contamination (article I.6). It covers such oil both as cargo and in the bunkers of such a ship. So on a voyage with a crude or fuel-oil parcel, the tanker is a CLC 'ship' and needs a CLC certificate - required by article VII once she carries more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo.

Bunkers 2001 covers contamination damage from the ship's own fuel (article 1.5), but article 4.1 disapplies it to anything that is CLC pollution damage. So it governs her bunkers precisely on the voyages when she is not a CLC ship - when she is carrying only non-persistent products such as gasoline or naphtha, or is clean of persistent residues. The certificate is required of a registered owner of a ship over 1,000 gross tonnage (article 7).

HNS covers the cargo in every case the other two do not reach. Non-persistent oil products are outside CLC's definition of oil but squarely inside HNS categories (i) and (vi). And even with a persistent oil cargo, fire and explosion damage is not 'pollution damage' under CLC, which is confined to contamination - so article 4.3(a) does not exclude it and HNS answers for it.

blocks.p: A products tanker trades across all of these states, often within a single charter: persistent one voyage, light distillate the next, in ballast with residues in between. No one certificate follows her through that cycle, and none of the three regimes will answer for a gap that belongs to another. She therefore carries all three so that, whatever she is loaded with and however the casualty develops, there is an identified insurer and a certificate to found a direct action against.

blocks.h: 7. c) The certificate itself, and the two tiers behind it

blocks.p: Under article 12.1 the owner of a ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS must maintain insurance or other financial security in the sums fixed by applying the article 9.1 limits. Article 12.2 requires a compulsory insurance certificate in the model form of Annex I, issued or certified by the State of the ship's registry, naming the ship, the owner, the IMO ship identification number, the type and duration of security and the insurer. It must be carried on board (12.4), it is mutually recognised by other States Parties (12.7), and a claim may be brought directly against the insurer (12.8).

Behind the certificate sits the two-tier structure. Tier one is the owner's strict liability under article 7, limited by article 9.1 to 100 million units of account for bulk HNS and 115 million where packaged HNS is or may be involved. Tier two is the HNS Fund, financed by receivers of contributing cargo, which under article 14 pays where no liability arises, where the owner is financially incapable, or where the damage exceeds his limit - the total of both tiers being capped at 250 million units of account for any one incident. Claims are time-barred under article 37 after three years from knowledge of the damage and in no case later than ten years from the incident.

The three limbs are worth 6, 5 and 5, and they are not equally hard. Limb (a) is recall and can be earned in full by anyone who has learned the seven categories with their parent instruments - it is the most reliably scoring six marks in the question. Limb (b) looks like recall and is not: the marks sit in noticing that the definition is wider than pollution. Limb (c) is the discriminating limb. It cannot be answered by describing three conventions in turn; it has to explain why one ship needs all three, which means identifying the variable each convention is drawn around.

blocks.h: The design idea behind article 1.5 - definition by reference

blocks.p: The Convention never says 'benzene' or 'LNG'. It says: whatever is in IBC chapter 17, whatever is in IGC chapter 19, whatever the IMDG Code covers in packaged form, and so on. This is deliberate and worth understanding rather than memorising. A closed commodity list written in 1996 would have been obsolete within a decade; a list of pointers updates itself every time those codes are amended. It also means a candidate who knows the codes already knows most of the HNS definition - the examiner is testing whether you can see the connection, not whether you have memorised a separate list.

The one phrase to underline in article 1.5(a) is 'carried on board a ship as cargo'. Almost every boundary question in this topic - bunkers, stores, residues, ballast - is answered by that phrase before any exclusion article is reached.

blocks.h: Why 'damage' is wider here than under CLC and Bunkers

blocks.p: Compare the three definitions side by side and the point becomes obvious. CLC article I.6(a): loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination. Bunkers article 1.9(a): loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination. HNS article 1.6: (a) loss of life or personal injury on board or outside the ship - no mention of contamination; (b) loss of or damage to property outside the ship - no mention of contamination; only head (c) speaks of contamination, and it is the environmental head.

That is not drafting untidiness. Oil pollution harms by coating; chemicals and gases harm by burning, exploding, reacting and poisoning, and they harm the ship's own crew as much as anyone ashore - which is why head (a) reaches injury on board, something neither oil convention does. If you write HNS as 'the chemical version of CLC' you have missed the whole of limb (b).

blocks.h: The bunkers point - an exclusion that is not there

blocks.p: Many summaries state that the HNS Convention 'does not apply to damage covered by the Bunkers Convention'. That proposition does not appear in the Convention. Article 4.3 contains exactly two exclusions - CLC pollution damage, and class 7 radioactive material - and the word 'bunker' appears nowhere in the instrument. Bunker oil is outside HNS for a more fundamental reason: article 1.5(a) covers only substances carried as cargo, and a ship's own fuel is not cargo. The distinction matters because it tells you what happens at the edges - residues of a previous cargo are expressly brought back in by article 1.5(b), whereas fuel never enters the definition at all.

blocks.h: Limb (c) worked through - the three variables

blocks.p: Set out the axis each convention is drawn around and the answer writes itself:

ul: CLC 92 - drawn around a substance (persistent oil) and a mechanism (contamination). Note that it covers the tanker's own bunkers as well as her cargo, because article I.5 says 'whether carried on board a ship as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship'. And she is only a CLC 'ship' while actually carrying oil in bulk as cargo, or on a following voyage with residues aboard.

Bunkers 2001 - drawn around a function (oil used for the operation or propulsion of the ship) and the same mechanism (contamination). Article 4.1 stands it down wherever CLC pollution damage applies, so it fills the gap left when the tanker is not a CLC ship.

HNS - drawn around cargo and a much wider set of mechanisms. It picks up the two things the other two cannot reach: non-persistent oil products, which are outside CLC's definition of oil altogether, and non-contamination damage such as fire and explosion, which is outside CLC's definition of pollution damage even when the cargo is persistent.

blocks.p: So a products tanker on a rotation of crude, then gasoline, then a chemical parcel, moves between all three regimes without changing anything about herself. That is the answer to 'why all three', and it is worth stating explicitly in the script rather than leaving the examiner to infer it.

ul: Treating HNS as a pollution convention and confining limb (b) to spills and contamination.
Listing commodities instead of the seven categories with their parent instruments. The instrument reference is the mark.
Saying the Convention excludes bunker oil by an exclusion article. It does not - bunkers are simply not cargo.
Forgetting residues under article 1.5(b), which is the most commonly dropped part of limb (a).
Omitting that head (a) covers personal injury on board - a real difference from the oil conventions.
Answering limb (c) by describing three conventions separately instead of explaining why one ship needs all three.
Quoting a number of Contracting States, or an entry-into-force date. Neither was available at this sitting and the question does not ask for either.

The stem's premise - 'is expected shortly to come into force' - is the examiner telling you the state of play. Answer inside it. An answer that corrects the examiner with a later date is answering a different paper.
'List and give examples' in limb (a) means both. Categories without examples, or examples without categories, each lose half the limb.

'Types of pollution and subsequent losses or damages' - the word 'pollution' in the stem is the trap. The Convention's own heading is damage, and it is wider than pollution. Answer what the Convention covers, not what the word in the stem suggests.
Limb (c) says 'probably require'. The examiner is inviting the trading-pattern reasoning, not a categorical assertion that every products tanker always carries all three.

blocks.p: For limb (a), walk the ship: oil tanks (i), chemical tanks (ii) and (iii), gas tanks (v), light products (vi), the holds (vii), the containers on deck (iv) - then remember that the empty tank still counts, which is residues (1.5(b)). For limb (b), the four heads are PEOPLE, PROPERTY, ENVIRONMENT, PREVENTION - and only the third one says contamination. For limb (c): persistent + contamination = CLC; my own fuel = Bunkers; everything else, including fire = HNS.

HNS article 1.6 - the four heads of damage.

quick_revision.recall_15s: What it is. The 1996 Convention as amended by the 2010 Protocol, read as one instrument - strict owner liability, compulsory insurance and a cargo-financed second tier, doing for hazardous cargoes what CLC and the Fund do for persistent oil. At this sitting it was not yet in force, and the question says so. (a) Substances - article 1.5(a), defined by reference to other IMO instruments and covering only what is carried as cargo: (i) oils in bulk per MARPOL Annex I reg 1; (ii) noxious liquid substances in bulk per Annex II reg 1.10 plus provisional categories X, Y, Z; (iii) dangerous liquids in bulk in IBC Code chapter 17; (iv) packaged dangerous goods under the IMDG Code; (v) liquefied gases in IGC Code chapter 19; (vi) liquids in bulk with flashpoint not exceeding 60°C; (vii) solid bulk materials with chemical hazards under the IMSBC Code. Article 1.5(b) adds residues. Bulk HNS (1.5bis) is everything but (iv); packaged HNS (1.5ter) is (iv). (b) Damage - article 1.6: loss of life or personal injury on board or outside; property damage outside the ship; contamination of the environment, with impairment limited to reasonable reinstatement costs; and costs of preventive measures. The key point: heads (a) and (b) are not limited to contamination, so fire, explosion and toxicity are covered - unlike CLC and Bunkers, which are contamination regimes. Excluded: CLC pollution damage (article 4.3(a), whether or not compensation is payable under CLC); class 7 radioactive material (4.3(b)); contract-of-carriage claims (4.1); warships (4.4). Bunkers are not excluded by any article - they are simply not cargo. (c) Three certificates because the regime changes with the parcel: CLC covers only persistent oil and only contamination, but covers her bunkers too while she is a CLC ship; Bunkers 2001 covers her fuel on the voyages when she is not (article 4.1 stands it down where CLC applies), for ships over 1,000 GT; and HNS covers non-persistent products, which are outside CLC's 'oil' altogether, and fire and explosion damage from any oil cargo, which is outside CLC's 'pollution damage'. Certificate: article 12 - Annex I model form, issued by the flag State, carried on board, mutually recognised, direct action against the insurer. Limits: article 9 - 100 million units of account bulk, 115 million packaged; HNS Fund to a combined 250 million; time bar 3 years / 10 years under article 37.

quick_revision.major_trap: Answering as though HNS were another pollution convention. It is not. Article 1.6 heads (a) and (b) carry no reference to contamination, so fire, explosion, toxicity and reactivity - the ways chemical and gas cargoes actually kill and destroy - are squarely covered, and limb (b) asks for exactly that breadth. The second trap is stating that HNS excludes bunker oil by an exclusion: it does not, and the word 'bunker' appears nowhere in the Convention. Bunkers fall outside because article 1.5(a) covers only substances carried as cargo. The third trap is temporal and the examiner has already set it in the stem - the Convention was not in force at this sitting and the stem says it was 'expected shortly to come into force'. Write the answer in that posture. Do not import a later entry-into-force date, a later ratification, or a count of Contracting States.

questions.understand_first: Start from the gap the Convention was written to fill. Persistent oil already had CLC and the Fund. Everything else a ship carries - chemicals, gases, packaged dangerous goods, light products, hazardous solids - had no international liability regime at all, and those cargoes do not usually cause harm by contaminating a shoreline. They burn, explode, react and poison. So the drafters did two things: they defined the cargo by pointing at the codes that already regulate it rather than writing a list that would date, and they defined damage more widely than the oil conventions, without the word contamination in the personal-injury and property heads. Hold those two design choices and both limb (a) and limb (b) follow from them. Limb (c) is then simply the seam: three conventions, each drawn round a different variable, and a products tanker that crosses all three seams in the ordinary course of her trade.

retrieval_cards.why: Steps 2 and 3 are limb (a), steps 4 and 5 limb (b), steps 6 and 7 limb (c). The marks split 6 / 5 / 5.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does article 1.5 define hazardous and noxious substances?
retrieval_cards.answer: As substances, materials and articles carried on board a ship as cargo in seven categories, each defined by reference to another IMO instrument: oils in bulk (MARPOL Annex I); noxious liquid substances in bulk (Annex II); dangerous liquids in bulk (IBC Code chapter 17); packaged dangerous goods (IMDG Code); liquefied gases (IGC Code chapter 19); liquids with a flashpoint not exceeding 60 degrees C; and solid bulk materials with chemical hazards (IMSBC Code). Article 1.5(b) adds residues.
retrieval_cards.why: Definition by reference rather than by commodity list is the design idea of the whole Convention, and the instrument names are where the marks are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is HNS damage wider than CLC or Bunkers pollution damage?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because in article 1.6 only head (c), the environmental head, refers to contamination. Head (a), loss of life or personal injury on board or outside the ship, and head (b), loss of or damage to property outside the ship, carry no such limitation. So fire, explosion, toxicity and reactivity are covered, and injury to the ship's own crew is covered. CLC article I.6 and Bunkers article 1.9 are both confined to damage caused by contamination.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the analytical heart of limb (b) and the commonest thing candidates miss by treating HNS as a pollution convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the HNS Convention exclude bunker oil, and by which article?
retrieval_cards.answer: It does not exclude it by any article. The word 'bunker' does not appear in the Convention. Article 4.3 contains only two exclusions - CLC pollution damage, and class 7 radioactive material. Bunker oil is outside HNS because article 1.5(a) covers only substances carried as cargo, and a ship's own fuel is not cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: A widely repeated summary states this as an exclusion. It is not in the text, and the real mechanism is more useful because it also answers residues, stores and ballast.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why would one products tanker need CLC, Bunker and HNS certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the applicable regime changes with the parcel she carries. CLC covers only persistent oil and only contamination. Bunkers 2001 covers her own fuel on the voyages when she is not a CLC ship, article 4.1 standing it down where CLC applies. HNS covers non-persistent products, outside CLC's 'oil', and fire or explosion from any oil cargo, outside CLC's 'pollution damage'. No one certificate follows her through that cycle.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) carries five marks and cannot be earned by describing the three conventions separately - the mark is in the seam between them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the HNS limits of liability and the time bars.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 9.1(a): bulk HNS from 10 million units of account, capped at 100 million. Article 9.1(b): packaged or mixed HNS from 11.5 million, capped at 115 million. Article 14.5: the Fund and the owner together capped at 250 million per incident. Article 37: three years from knowledge of the damage, and in no case later than ten years from the incident.
retrieval_cards.why: Three ceilings and two time limits; quoting the bulk cap for a packaged casualty is the usual slip.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does article 12 require, and what is on the certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: The owner of a ship registered in a State Party and actually carrying HNS must maintain insurance in the sums fixed by the article 9.1 limits. The certificate takes the Annex I model form and is issued or certified by the flag State, naming the ship, the owner, the IMO ship identification number, the type and duration of security and the insurer. It is carried on board, mutually recognised, and open to direct action against the insurer.
retrieval_cards.why: The certificate is the operational face of the Convention and the part a chief engineer actually sees on board.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What was the status of the Convention at this sitting, and what must not be written?
retrieval_cards.answer: It had not entered into force, and its entry-into-force conditions had not been met. The stem's own statement that it was expected shortly to come into force is the position at the sitting and is preserved. Do not import a later entry-into-force date, a later ratification, or any count of Contracting States - none of that existed on the day and none of it is asked for.

You are doing a Main engine decarbonisation and the work is carried out in two groups, one working on the cylinder head platform and the other group working in the bottom platform. Identify the areas in this operation where there can be a hazard due to failure of communication. Also suggest risk mitigation measures to mitigate the hazard of failure of communication.

blocks.p: Communication is the transfer of information, instructions and meaning from a sender to a receiver through a channel, understood by the receiver as the sender intended. It is complete not when the message is sent but when feedback confirms it was understood. That feedback loop is what distinguishes communication from broadcasting.

ul: Verbal - face to face, telephone, UHF/VHF, public address: fast, immediate feedback, no record.
Written - work orders, permits, risk assessments, checklists, night orders, log books, handovers: slower but auditable, and what the safety management system relies on.
Non-verbal - hand signals, body language, and the visual and audible alarm system. In high noise this becomes the primary channel.
Formal and informal - the first recorded and following the organisational chart; the second quicker but unverified.
Vertical and horizontal - downward orders, upward reports and concerns, lateral between departments. Upward communication fails first, and safety depends on it.
Internal and external, and electronic - ship to shore, port, VTS and class; email, planned maintenance systems and alarm data.
Physical - engine room noise, distance, hearing protection, radio dead spots, intervening structure.
Language and semantic - multinational crews, differing fluency, jargon. Addressed by the working language required under SOLAS V/14.3 and ISM element 6.
Hierarchical and cultural - reluctance to question a senior. This is the barrier most often behind an accident everybody could see coming.
Physiological - fatigue, hearing loss, stress, time pressure, complacency on a routine job.
Organisational - unclear responsibility, two people each believing the other is in charge, poor handover.
Assumption - believing a message was understood because nobody asked. Silence is not confirmation.

blocks.h: 4. Where communication failure becomes a hazard in this job

blocks.p: The defining feature is vertical separation with a shared machine between the two groups: each can alter the condition of the engine the other is working inside, and neither can see the other. Hence:

ul: Turning gear operated with a person in the crankcase or under a piston - the most serious risk in the job.
Starting air admitted, or the main starting air valve left un-isolated, with the engine opened up.
Dropped objects - tools, nuts or debris falling from the cylinder head platform onto the group below.
Uncoordinated lifting of a piston, liner or head through the space while men work beneath the load path.
Hydraulic tensioning tools pressurised while another person handles the studs or nuts.
Systems restored by a third party - a standby pump starting on auto, or the control room restoring a system, releasing hot oil or water onto open work.
Enclosed space entry to crankcase or scavenge space without the other group knowing anyone is inside.
Shift handover - the incoming group not knowing what is isolated, what is slack, and where people are.

blocks.h: 5. Risk mitigation - organise the job before it starts

ul: A risk assessment and permit to work, with a separate enclosed space entry permit for crankcase or scavenge space.
One named person in overall charge and one leader per group. Nobody moves the engine except on that person's order.
A joint toolbox talk before starting: sequence, who is where, isolations, communication plan and the stop-work rule.
Lock-out and tag-out of turning gear supply, starting air, hydraulic power pack and standby pumps, tagged at the control room and at every local starter, with the key held by the person in charge.

blocks.h: 6. Risk mitigation - the communication plan itself

ul: A dedicated radio channel for the job, with headsets compatible with hearing protection, tested before work begins.
Closed-loop communication as the standing rule - instruction given, repeated back, execution confirmed. Turning the engine is announced, acknowledged by both groups, and only then carried out.
Agreed standard phrases and a hand-signal set for when radios fail or noise defeats them.
Confirm understanding by asking a person to state back what they are about to do - never by asking "do you understand?"
An explicit stop-work authority for everyone, stated at the toolbox talk so that using it is expected rather than brave.

blocks.h: 7. Risk mitigation - physical and record controls

ul: Avoid work directly above and below where the sequence allows; otherwise an exclusion zone, gratings or covers, and tethered tools.
A written handover at each shift change and a job log of isolations, work done and personnel inside the engine.
A personnel tally for crankcase and scavenge space entry, checked before any isolation is removed.
Formal permit close-out, confirming all persons and tools clear before turning gear is disengaged and the engine restored.

blocks.p: Here the machine is the message path: what one group does is felt immediately by the other. The controls that matter are specific, not exhortations - one person in charge, isolation that a misunderstanding cannot undo, closed-loop confirmation before the engine moves, and a written handover. Communication failure in this job does not cause inconvenience; it causes fatalities.

This is four questions in one, and the marks follow the work. The first three limbs are standard theory that every candidate can write, so they do not discriminate - keep them tight and complete. The scenario limb is where the marks are actually won, because it requires you to apply the theory to a specific engineering operation. Give roughly half the answer to limbs 4 to 7. A candidate who writes three pages on types and barriers and then two generic lines about 'good communication' has answered the easy part of the question and missed the point of it.

blocks.h: The word decarbonisation means the overhaul, not GHG

blocks.p: Read the scenario carefully. In this question "Main engine decarbonisation" means the traditional overhaul job - removing carbon deposits, pistons, liners, exhaust valves and heads - with men on the cylinder head platform above and on the bottom platform below. It does not mean greenhouse gas decarbonisation, even though Q2 of this same paper is about CII and GHG reduction. Writing about carbon intensity here would lose the entire second half of the question. The tell is the physical description of two working platforms.

blocks.h: The organising idea for the scenario limb

blocks.p: One sentence carries the whole limb: two groups, vertically separated, working on one machine that either of them can move or pressurise. Every hazard is a consequence - what falls from above, what moves in between, and what a third party can restore from the control room. If you state that principle first and then derive the hazards, the list writes itself and reads as analysis rather than recall.

blocks.h: Where the authority for this answer comes from - and where it honestly does not

blocks.p: Worth understanding, because it is the difference between a confident answer and an invented one. Some limbs here are governed and some are not. The working-language requirement is real and citable - SOLAS regulation V/14.3, supported by ISM Code element 6. Procedures for shipboard operations, which is where permits and isolations live, sit in ISM element 7, and the alarm and emergency response in element 8. Leadership and teamworking are STCW management-level competences.

But no convention prescribes a taxonomy of communication types, and none lists the hazards of a two-platform decarbonisation. Those come from established practice, the Code of Safe Working Practices - which is industry guidance, not a convention - and ordinary engineering risk assessment. Say so rather than inventing a regulation number. An answer that declares its basis honestly reads as competent; one that attaches a fabricated regulation to a good engineering point destroys the credibility of everything around it.

ul: Misreading 'decarbonisation' as GHG reduction and losing the scenario limb entirely.
Listing barriers without saying which ones bite in an engine room. Noise, hearing protection and radio dead spots are the specific ones; hierarchy is the dangerous one.

Giving mitigations that are slogans - 'improve communication', 'hold meetings'. Marks come from named controls: permit to work, lock-out/tag-out, closed-loop confirmation, exclusion zone, written handover.
Forgetting the third party. Many real accidents come from the engine control room or another watch restoring a system, not from either working group.
Defining communication without feedback. A definition that stops at 'transfer of information' misses the element every subsequent barrier attacks.
Attaching an invented regulation number to the communication theory. The theory limbs are not prescribed by any instrument, and saying so is stronger than pretending otherwise.

blocks.p:
"You briefed them - so you communicated, didn't you?" No. A briefing is transmission. Communication is complete only when understanding is confirmed, which is why the answer asks people to state back what they are about to do rather than asking whether they understood.

"Who may stop this job?" The expected answer is anyone. If you say only the Chief Engineer or the person in charge may stop it, you have described the hierarchical barrier you just finished criticising.

"Which single control would you keep if you could keep only one?" Physical isolation with lock-out and tag-out. Procedures depend on people communicating correctly; isolation survives a communication failure, which is exactly what is being guarded against.

ul: What is closed-loop communication? Instruction given, repeated back by the receiver, execution confirmed - so a misheard order is caught before it is acted on.

What must be isolated before crankcase entry on this job? Turning gear power supply, starting air, hydraulic power pack and standby lubricating oil and cooling water pumps, locked and tagged, with the key controlled.
Where is the working language requirement? SOLAS regulation V/14.3, supported by ISM Code element 6 on resources and personnel.
Why is upward communication the critical one? Because defects, doubts and refusals to proceed travel upward, and hierarchy suppresses them.
What do you record at handover? Isolations in place, work completed and in progress, tools and personnel inside the engine, and any change to the plan.

Does any convention list the hazards of this job? No. The controls come from the ship's safety management system under ISM, from the Code of Safe Working Practices as guidance, and from the risk assessment you carry out.

blocks.p: D-T-B then H-O-C-P. The theory: Define, Types, Barriers (steps 1 to 3). The application: Hazards (step 4), then three families of control - Organise the job (step 5), Communication plan (step 6), Physical and paper controls (step 7). Within the hazards, work top to bottom: what falls, what turns, what is pressurised, who else can restore a system.

ul: ISM Code element 6 - resources and personnel; effective communication and understanding in the working language
ISM Code element 7 - procedures for shipboard operations, which is where permits and isolation procedures sit
ISM Code element 8 - emergency preparedness, including how an alarm is raised from within the engine
SOLAS chapter V regulation 14.3 - working language established and recorded in the log book
STCW Code section A-VIII/2 and the management-level leadership and teamworking competences
Code of Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seafarers - permit to work, enclosed space entry, isolation and lock-out/tag-out practice (industry guidance, not a convention)

blocks.p: The regulatory references above are verified. The hazard identification and the control measures are generic good practice, not a specific ship's procedure: isolation points, lifting arrangements, permit forms and radio discipline differ between engine types and between company safety management systems, and the ship's own SMS governs. The list of hazards is not claimed to be exhaustive - a real job requires its own risk assessment with the people who will do it. Where this answer names a control, it is describing what a competent management-level engineer should expect to see, not asserting that any particular convention mandates that specific control. Nothing in this answer is time-sensitive: the instruments cited are long-standing and the mechanics of an engine overhaul do not change with an amendment cycle.

The organising fact is vertical separation with a shared machine: two groups who cannot see each other, each able to move, pressurise or flood the engine the other is inside. Hazards: turning gear operated with a person in the crankcase or under a piston; starting air admitted or not isolated; dropped objects from the platform above; uncoordinated lifting of a piston, liner or head through the space; hydraulic tensioning tools pressurised while another handles the nuts; a third party restoring a system - standby pump on auto, or the control room; enclosed space entry unknown to the other group; and shift handover gaps. Controls, in three families. Organise: risk assessment and permit to work with a separate enclosed-space permit; one named person in overall charge and nobody moves the engine except on that order; a joint toolbox talk; and lock-out/tag-out of turning gear, starting air, hydraulic power pack and standby pumps, tagged at the control room and every local starter, key held by the person in charge. Communicate: a dedicated radio channel tested before work; closed-loop communication as the standing rule, so turning the engine is announced, acknowledged by both groups and only then done; agreed standard phrases and hand signals; confirm by asking a person to state back what they are about to do, never 'do you understand?'; and explicit stop-work authority for everyone. Physical and record: avoid work directly above and below, else an exclusion zone, gratings, covers and tethered tools; a written handover and job log; a personnel tally checked before any isolation is removed; and formal permit close-out before the engine is restored. The point: the machine is the message path, and isolation survives a communication failure when a procedure does not.

blocks.h: 1. The background - the gap the Convention was written to close

blocks.p: By the 1990s the international liability architecture had a conspicuous hole in it. CLC 92 answered for oil pollution, but only from a ship constructed or adapted for the carriage of oil in bulk as cargo (article I.1) and only for persistent oil (article I.5). Every other ship - bulk carriers, container ships, car carriers, cruise ships - fell outside it entirely, and yet a large container ship or bulk carrier routinely bunkers several thousand tonnes of heavy fuel oil, more than the entire cargo of a small product tanker. A bunker spill from such a ship left claimants to whatever national law and ordinary tort principles offered: no strict liability, no compulsory insurance, no certificate, and often no solvent defendant. The International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage was adopted on 23 March 2001 to close that gap and entered into force on 21 November 2008.

blocks.h: 2. Its relevance - where it sits in the liability architecture

blocks.p: Its relevance is that it completes a three-part scheme in which each instrument is drawn around a different variable and the three are mutually exclusive: CLC 92 for persistent oil carried as cargo by a tanker, and that tanker's own bunkers; Bunkers 2001 for the fuel of every other ship; and the HNS Convention for hazardous and noxious cargoes. It deliberately borrows CLC's architecture - strict liability, limited liability, compulsory insurance, a certificate and direct action against the insurer - so that the same commercial machinery, and the same P&I 'blue card' practice, could be extended without a new institution. It has no cargo-financed second tier: there is no bunker equivalent of the IOPC Fund.

The two definitions are deliberately parallel. Under Bunkers article 1.9, and CLC article I.6, 'pollution damage' means loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of oil, with compensation for impairment of the environment other than loss of profit confined to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken, together with the costs of preventive measures and further loss or damage caused by them. Both are therefore contamination regimes, and neither reaches fire or explosion damage.
The differences are in the substance and the boundary:

ul: What oil. CLC covers only persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil - crude, fuel oil, heavy diesel, lubricating oil - whether as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship. Bunkers covers any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and its residues, so it is not confined to persistent oil and picks up a marine gas oil spill that CLC would not.

The principal exclusion. By article 4.1 the Bunkers Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is actually payable under it. The two can never overlap, and the exclusion turns on the CLC definition, not on the outcome of a claim - so a claimant who fails under CLC cannot fall back on Bunkers.
Other exclusions. Warships, naval auxiliaries and State non-commercial ships (Bunkers article 4.2; CLC article XI), unless the State opts in.
Geographic scope. Both apply in the territory and territorial sea and in the exclusive economic zone of a State Party (Bunkers article 2), with preventive measures covered wherever taken.

blocks.p: Here the two are identical, and the symmetry is worth stating expressly. Under Bunkers article 8 and CLC article VIII, rights to compensation are extinguished unless an action is brought within three years from the date when the damage occurred; and in no case may an action be brought more than six years from the date of the incident which caused the damage. Where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six-year period runs from the first of them.

Two points earn the marks. First, these are extinction periods, not procedural limitation - the right itself ceases, so it cannot be revived by agreement or waiver in the way a domestic limitation defence sometimes can. Secondly, the three years run from when the damage occurred, not from when the claimant knew of it - which is stricter than the HNS Convention, where article 37 runs three years from knowledge and allows ten years absolute.

Both impose strict liability on the shipowner at the time of the incident - Bunkers article 3.1, CLC article III.1 - subject to the same three narrow defences, which the owner must prove: an act of war, hostilities, civil war, insurrection or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party's intentional act or omission; or damage wholly caused by the negligence or wrongful act of an authority responsible for the maintenance of navigational aids. In both, contributory intent or negligence of the claimant may exonerate the owner wholly or partly.
But who is liable is the single greatest difference between the two conventions, and it runs in opposite directions:

ul: CLC channels liability inward. Liability attaches to the registered owner alone, and article III.4 expressly bars any claim against the crew, pilot, salvor, and against any charterer (howsoever described, including a bareboat charterer), manager or operator - unless they acted with intent or recklessly with knowledge. The claimant has one certain defendant and no more.

Bunkers spreads liability outward. Article 1.3 defines 'shipowner' to mean the owner including the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, and article 3.2 makes their liability joint and several. The claimant may pursue any or all of them.

blocks.p: The practical consequence is real: under CLC the manager and the bareboat charterer are protected, and under the Bunkers Convention the very same parties are exposed. Where an incident involves two or more ships, the shipowners of all of them are jointly and severally liable for damage that is not reasonably separable (Bunkers article 5; CLC article IV).

blocks.h: 6. c) Limitation of liability - the structural difference

ul: CLC carries its own limits. By article V.1 the owner may limit to 4,510,000 units of account for a ship not exceeding 5,000 units of tonnage, plus 631 units of account for each additional ton, subject to an overall ceiling of 89,770,000 units of account. The fund is constituted with the court under article V.3, and once constituted the owner's other assets are protected and any arrested ship must be released (article VI). The right to limit is lost under article V.2 where the damage resulted from the owner's personal act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.

The Bunkers Convention carries no limits at all. Article 6 merely preserves the right to limit 'under any applicable national or international regime, such as the Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976, as amended'. There is no bunker-specific figure and no bunker-specific fund.

blocks.p: This is not a drafting convenience but the substantive weakness of the regime, and it is the point a management-level answer should make. Because limitation is left to the LLMC, a bunker-pollution claim competes in a general limitation fund shared with all other claims arising from the same incident - wreck removal, cargo, personal injury - rather than drawing on a dedicated pollution fund as it would under CLC. The available compensation is correspondingly less certain, it varies between States according to which limitation regime each has adopted, and there is no second tier to make up any shortfall.

blocks.h: 7. d) Compulsory insurance and financial security

ul: Who must insure, and the threshold. Under Bunkers article 7.1 the registered owner of a ship of more than 1,000 gross tonnage registered in a State Party must maintain insurance or other financial security covering the registered owner's liability, in an amount equal to the limits of the applicable limitation regime but not exceeding the LLMC figure. Under CLC article VII.1 the obligation arises instead from the cargo - an owner whose ship carries more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo must insure in the sums fixed by article V.1. So the two thresholds are measured in different units: ship size against cargo quantity.

A deliberate asymmetry. Liability under Bunkers article 3 attaches to the wide 'shipowner' group, but the insurance duty falls on the registered owner only. The bareboat charterer and manager may be sued and are not required to insure.

The certificate. In both regimes a certificate in the annexed model form is issued or certified by the flag State, naming the ship, the owner, the IMO ship identification number, the type and duration of security and the insurer. It must be carried on board (Bunkers article 7.5), and security may not lapse on less than three months' notice (article 7.6). A State Party may delegate issue to a recognised organisation (article 7.3). In practice the P&I club issues a 'blue card' evidencing cover, on which the State issues the certificate.

Direct action. Under Bunkers article 7.10 and CLC article VII.8 a claim may be brought directly against the insurer. The insurer may invoke the shipowner's defences other than bankruptcy, may plead the shipowner's wilful misconduct, and - importantly - may limit to the insured amount even if the shipowner has lost the right to limit.

Enforcement reach. A flag State may not permit a ship to operate without a certificate (article 7.11), and by article 7.12 every State Party must ensure that security is in force for any ship over 1,000 gt wherever registered entering or leaving its ports. That is why the certificate is carried by ships of non-party flags as a practical matter, and it is what gives the Convention near-universal effect at the port-State level.

blocks.p: The stem sets a background plus four limbs of four marks each, and it says 'comparing with' CLC 92. That word governs the whole answer. Four separate descriptions of the Bunkers Convention, however accurate, cannot score well because they do not do what was asked. The efficient shape is to take each limb as a contrast: state the common rule once, then the difference. Two of the four limbs are genuinely identical between the conventions - time limits, and the three defences - and saying so explicitly is worth marks, because it demonstrates you checked rather than assumed.

blocks.h: The one idea that generates the whole answer

blocks.p: CLC attaches to a cargo; the Bunkers Convention attaches to a ship's own fuel. Everything else follows. A cargo can be measured, so CLC's insurance threshold is 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo; fuel cannot usefully be, so Bunkers uses 1,000 gross tonnage. A tanker owner is a single identifiable defendant with predictable insurance, so CLC can channel liability to him and protect the charterer and manager; the operator of a general cargo ship may sit behind layers of management companies, so Bunkers casts the net wider. A tanker casualty is overwhelmingly a pollution event, so CLC can justify a dedicated limitation fund and a second tier; a bunker spill usually accompanies a grounding or collision generating many other claims, so Bunkers leaves limitation to the general LLMC regime.

blocks.h: The limitation point, which is where most answers go wrong

blocks.p: It is worth being precise, because this is the most commonly misstated proposition in the topic. The Bunkers Convention contains no limitation figures whatsoever. Article 6 reads that nothing in the Convention shall affect the right to limit 'under any applicable national or international regime, such as the Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976, as amended'. That is the entire limitation provision.

Three consequences follow, and stating them is what turns a recall answer into an analytical one. First, the amount available varies between States according to which limitation regime each has adopted, so compensation is not uniform in the way CLC compensation is. Secondly, the pollution claim is not ring-fenced: it shares a general limitation fund with wreck removal, cargo and personal injury claims arising from the same casualty, and may be substantially diluted. Thirdly, there is no second tier - no bunker equivalent of the IOPC Fund - so once the LLMC fund is exhausted there is nothing behind it. A major bunker spill from a very large non-tanker can therefore leave claimants materially worse off than the same spill from a laden tanker.

This answer does not quote an LLMC figure. That is deliberate: article 6 refers out rather than fixing a number, so a single figure would misdescribe the mechanism, and the comparison turns on the referral itself rather than on any particular amount.

blocks.h: Channelling - and the trap of getting it backwards

blocks.p: Under CLC article III.4 no claim may be made against the crew, the pilot, a salvor, or 'any charterer (howsoever described, including a bareboat charterer), manager or operator of the ship' unless they acted with intent or recklessly with knowledge. Liability is channelled to the registered owner. Under Bunkers article 1.3 the word 'shipowner' is defined to mean the owner 'including the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator', and article 3.2 makes them jointly and severally liable.

So the identical parties - bareboat charterer, manager, operator - are protected by one convention and exposed by the other. Candidates who have learned CLC well are the ones most likely to get this wrong, because they carry the channelling rule across. If you remember only one contrast from this question, make it this one.

Both are confined to damage by contamination. Neither reaches fire or explosion damage, and neither reaches damage from anything that is not oil. That is precisely the space the HNS Convention was written to occupy, and a sentence placing all three instruments together is a good way to close the answer - it shows the examiner you understand the architecture rather than two isolated conventions.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Background. CLC 92 reaches only a ship constructed or adapted to carry oil in bulk as cargo, and only persistent oil. Every other ship - bulk carrier, box ship, cruise ship - carries thousands of tonnes of fuel and fell entirely outside it: no strict liability, no compulsory insurance, no certificate. The Bunkers Convention was adopted 23 March 2001 and entered into force 21 November 2008 to close that gap, borrowing CLC's architecture but with no second tier. (a) Pollution damage: both define it as loss or damage outside the ship by contamination, with environmental impairment limited to reasonable reinstatement costs, plus preventive measures. Differences: CLC covers persistent oil only; bunker oil is any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lube oil, used or intended for the operation or propulsion of the ship, plus residues - so not limited to persistent. Article 4.1 disapplies Bunkers to CLC pollution damage whether or not compensation is payable, so the two never overlap. Warships out; scope covers territorial sea and EEZ. (b) Time limits - identical: three years from when the damage occurred, and in no case more than six years from the incident, running from the first of a series. These extinguish the right. Contrast HNS: three years from knowledge, ten years absolute. (c) Liability: strict in both, same three defences - war or exceptional natural phenomenon, wholly a third party's intentional act, wholly the fault of a navigational-aid authority. The big difference is who: CLC channels inward to the registered owner and article III.4 bars claims against the charterer, manager or operator; Bunkers spreads outward - article 1.3 defines shipowner to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, jointly and severally liable under article 3.2. Limitation: CLC has its own figures - 4,510,000 units of account to 5,000 tons, plus 631 per ton, capped at 89,770,000 - lost on personal intent or recklessness. Bunkers has none: article 6 refers out to the LLMC 1976 as amended, so the claim shares a general fund with wreck removal, cargo and injury claims. (d) Insurance: Bunkers keys to ship size - registered owner, over 1,000 gt; CLC keys to cargo - more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo. Certificate in the annexed model form, carried on board, three months' notice before security lapses, blue card from the club, direct action against the insurer who may limit even if the owner cannot, and by article 7.12 port States enforce it on ships of any flag.

quick_revision.major_trap: Writing that the Bunkers Convention has its own limits of liability. It does not. Article 6 sets no figure at all and merely preserves the right to limit under any applicable regime, such as the LLMC 1976 as amended. That single fact is the substantive weakness of the whole regime - the claim competes in a general limitation fund shared with wreck removal, cargo and injury claims instead of a dedicated pollution fund, and there is no second tier to top it up. The second trap is getting the liable party backwards: CLC channels liability inward to the registered owner and expressly protects the charterer, manager and operator, whereas Bunkers spreads it outward to all of them jointly and severally. Candidates routinely state the CLC channelling rule and then apply it to the Bunkers Convention, which reverses the answer. The third trap is treating either convention as covering fire or explosion - both are confined to damage by contamination.

questions.understand_first: Read the two conventions as the same machine fitted to two different problems. The machinery is identical and was copied deliberately: strict liability, narrow defences, limited liability, compulsory insurance, a certificate and direct action against the insurer. What differs is what each is bolted to. CLC is bolted to a cargo - persistent oil in a tanker - so its thresholds are measured in tons of cargo, and because a tanker owner is a known, insurable, single defendant it can safely channel all liability to him and protect everyone else. Bunkers is bolted to a ship's own fuel, which every ship has, so its threshold is measured in gross tonnage; and because operating structures are opaque it does the opposite, casting the net over owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator together. Once you see that one difference - what each convention is attached to - the four limbs stop being a list to memorise and become consequences.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Bunkers Convention comparison question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The background and the gap it closed. 2 Where it sits in the liability architecture. 3 Limb (a) pollution damage and exclusions. 4 Limb (b) time limits. 5 Limb (c) who is liable. 6 Limb (c) limitation of liability. 7 Limb (d) compulsory insurance and financial security.
retrieval_cards.why: Background and relevance are a separate demand before the four printed limbs, and each limb is a contrast rather than a description.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do the two conventions define the oil they cover?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC article I.5: persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil such as crude, fuel oil, heavy diesel and lubricating oil, whether carried as cargo or in the bunkers of such a ship. Bunkers article 1.5: any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues. Bunker oil is therefore not limited to persistent oil.
retrieval_cards.why: The persistence limit is the reason a marine gas oil spill can fall under Bunkers but never under CLC.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the Bunkers Convention's limits of liability?
retrieval_cards.answer: It has none. Article 6 sets no figure and merely preserves the right to limit under any applicable national or international regime, such as the LLMC 1976 as amended. So the claim shares a general limitation fund with wreck removal, cargo and injury claims from the same casualty, the amount varies between States, and there is no second tier behind it.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most misstated proposition in this topic, and the substantive weakness of the whole regime.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who is liable under each convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC channels liability inward: the registered owner alone, and article III.4 bars claims against any charterer including a bareboat charterer, manager or operator. Bunkers spreads it outward: article 1.3 defines shipowner to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, and article 3.2 makes them jointly and severally liable.
retrieval_cards.why: The same parties are protected by one convention and exposed by the other. Carrying the CLC channelling rule across is the commonest error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the time limits under both conventions.
retrieval_cards.answer: Identical. Bunkers article 8 and CLC article VIII: three years from the date when the damage occurred, and in no case more than six years from the date of the incident, the six years running from the first of a series of occurrences. They extinguish the right rather than barring the remedy. HNS article 37 differs - three years from knowledge, ten years absolute.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying expressly that they are identical shows the comparison was checked rather than assumed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What triggers the compulsory insurance duty in each convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Bunkers article 7.1 keys to ship size: the registered owner of a ship of more than 1,000 gross tonnage registered in a State Party. CLC article VII.1 keys to cargo: an owner whose ship carries more than 2,000 tons of oil in bulk as cargo. Under Bunkers the liability is wide but the insurance duty falls on the registered owner alone.
retrieval_cards.why: Two thresholds measured in different units, and an asymmetry between who may be sued and who must insure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the certificate work, and can the insurer be sued directly?
retrieval_cards.answer: The flag State issues or certifies a certificate in the annexed model form, naming the ship, owner, IMO number, type and duration of security and insurer; it is carried on board and security may not lapse on less than three months' notice. The P&I club's blue card evidences cover. Under article 7.10 a claim may be brought directly against the insurer, who may limit even if the shipowner cannot.
retrieval_cards.why: Direct action plus the insurer's independent right to limit is what makes the certificate commercially meaningful.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does either convention cover fire or explosion damage from oil?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Both CLC article I.6 and Bunkers article 1.9 confine pollution damage to loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination, together with the costs of preventive measures. Fire and explosion damage falls outside both, and is one of the gaps the HNS Convention was written to fill.
retrieval_cards.why: Both are contamination regimes, and the point also supplies the closing sentence placing the three conventions together.
