blocks.h: 1. a) The human element, and how IMO and ILO divide the work

blocks.p: The human element is not one topic but the recognition that the great majority of casualties originate in human performance rather than in equipment failure. IMO frames it through resolution A.947(23), Human Element Vision, Principles and Goals, adopted 27 November 2003, which treats it as a complex, multi-dimensional issue spanning ships' crews, shore management, regulators, recognized organizations, shipyards and legislators, all of whom must co-operate.

The division of labour between the two organisations should be stated at the outset, because it explains why two separate regimes exist. IMO regulates the seafarer as the operator of a ship - competence, watchkeeping, fitness for duty and safe operation. ILO regulates the seafarer as a worker - employment, wages, hours, accommodation, welfare and social protection. Neither is complete on its own, and the two interlock precisely where working conditions become safety conditions: hours of rest appear in both, because a seafarer's terms of employment and the safety of the ship are the same question asked twice.

blocks.h: 2. The IMO regime - competence, safe operation and fitness for duty

ul: STCW 1978, as amended, most significantly by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force 1 January 2012, is the competence instrument. Its Part A tables specify for each function and level the competence required, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency behind it, the methods of demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so assessment is against a published standard. Part A is mandatory, Part B is guidance. Manila added mandatory training in leadership and teamworking and, at management level, leadership and managerial skill, which is where engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management enter the Convention.

STCW also regulates the physical human being: regulation I/9 medical fitness standards, regulation VIII/1 requiring Administrations, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and regulation VIII/2 governing watchkeeping arrangements. Manila also introduced alcohol limits.

Regulation I/14 places the duty on the company - valid certificates, familiarisation with the ship and her arrangements, and maintained documentation - so the human element is not left as the individual's problem. Regulations I/6, I/8 and I/11 govern training and assessment, quality standards systems and revalidation.

The ISM Code supplies the organisational half: element 6 resources and personnel, including qualification, familiarisation and a working language; element 8 emergency preparedness, drills and exercises; and element 9 reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences - the reporting culture without which human-element failures are never learned from.

Manning is the point at which the two regimes meet most directly. SOLAS regulation V/14 requires ships to be sufficiently and efficiently manned and the flag State to issue a minimum safe manning document, the principles being set out in IMO resolution A.1047(27), Principles of Minimum Safe Manning, adopted 30 November 2011. MLC Regulation 2.7 imposes the same requirement from the labour side.

blocks.h: 3. The ILO regime - MLC 2006, the fourth pillar

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 was adopted at the 94th (Maritime) Session of the International Labour Conference and consolidated some sixty-eight earlier ILO maritime instruments into one. It is universally described as the fourth pillar of the international regulatory regime, standing beside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW, and is often called the seafarers' bill of rights.

Its architecture is unusual and is worth a sentence. It has three parts: the Articles, setting out general obligations; the Regulations; and the Code. Article VI divides the Code in two - Part A contains Standards and is mandatory, while Part B contains Guidelines, not mandatory but to which Members must give due consideration. Article VI.3 adds substantial equivalence, allowing a Member to implement a Part A Standard differently provided the provision is substantially equivalent in achieving its general object and purpose. Article IV states the underlying rights: a safe and secure workplace, fair terms of employment, decent working and living conditions, and health protection, medical care, welfare measures and other forms of social protection.

The Regulations and Code are arranged in five Titles: 1 minimum requirements to work on a ship; 2 conditions of employment; 3 accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; 4 health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection; and 5 compliance and enforcement. The text operative at this sitting is the Convention as amended by the 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022 amendments, the 2022 set having entered into force on 23 December 2024 - nine months before this examination, and therefore simply the law.

blocks.h: 4. What the maritime labour and welfare regime actually requires

ul: Title 1 - who may go to sea. Standard A1.1.1 prohibits the employment of any person under 16; night work and hazardous work by those under 18 are prohibited. A valid medical certificate is required, valid for a maximum of two years, or one year under 18. Seafarers must be trained and qualified, and recruitment and placement services regulated - no fees are borne by the seafarer.

Title 2 - conditions of employment. The seafarers' employment agreement under Standard A2.1.1 is signed by both parties, the seafarer having an opportunity to examine it and seek advice before signing; a copy is carried on board for the seafarer and for inspectors. Hours of work and rest under Standard A2.3.5 require each Member to fix either maximum hours of work - 14 in any 24 and 72 in any seven days - or minimum hours of rest - 10 in any 24 and 77 in any seven days. Wages are paid at intervals no greater than monthly with a means of transmitting allotments home; repatriation arises on expiry abroad, on termination for justified reasons and on inability to perform duties, with a maximum service period on board of less than twelve months, backed by financial security for abandonment evidenced by a certificate carried on board.

Title 3 - accommodation and catering. Safe and decent accommodation, with the construction standards applying to ships built on or after entry into force for that Member. Standard A3.1 paragraph 17 requires recreational facilities, amenities and services including social connectivity, the associated guidance addressing internet access at reasonable charges - connectivity is a welfare requirement of the Convention, not a commercial courtesy. Food and drinking water of appropriate quality, nutritional value and quantity are supplied free of charge.

Title 4 - health, welfare and social protection. Medical care comparable to that available ashore and provided free of charge, including access to a doctor or dentist in ports of call where practicable. Shipowners' liability for sickness and injury in service, with financial security for contractual claims arising from death or long-term disability. On health and safety, Standard A4.3 paragraph 1(b) requires the provision of all necessary appropriately-sized personal protective equipment; Standard A4.3 paragraph 2 with Guideline B4.3.1 paragraph 3 requires that engineering and design control and the substitution of processes - replacing the dangerous by the less dangerous - take precedence over personal protective equipment, which is the hierarchy of controls made express in the Convention. Standard A4.3 paragraph 5(a) requires all deaths of seafarers to be investigated, recorded and reported annually to the Director-General of the International Labour Office for publication in a global register. Shore-based welfare facilities and social security complete the Title.

blocks.h: 5. Title 5 - what makes the labour regime enforceable

blocks.p: The flag State certifies. The maritime labour certificate is issued by the competent authority or by a recognized organization duly authorized, for a period not exceeding five years, subject to an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates. It is accompanied by the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance: Part I, drawn by the competent authority, listing the national requirements; and Part II, drawn by the shipowner, setting out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance between inspections. Appendix A5-I lists the sixteen matters that must be inspected and approved before certification.

In a foreign port, an authorized officer may inspect under Regulation 5.2.1. The certificate and DMLC are accepted as prima facie evidence of compliance and the inspection normally stops there; Standard A5.2.1.1 gives four triggers for a more detailed inspection - documents not produced, falsely maintained or invalid; clear grounds for believing conditions do not conform; reasonable grounds to believe the ship has changed flag to avoid compliance; or a complaint. Where conditions are clearly hazardous or the breach serious or repeated, the ship may be detained. Article V.7 supplies the commercial engine: ships of non-ratifying States must receive no more favourable treatment. Regulation 5.2.2 requires onshore complaint-handling procedures and Regulation 5.3 places duties on labour-supplying States such as India.

blocks.h: 6. Where the two organisations act jointly, and the state of the regime at this sitting

ul: The two organisations act together through joint ILO/IMO tripartite bodies, which produced the Guidelines on fair treatment of seafarers detained in connection with alleged crimes and the Guidelines on fair treatment of seafarers in the event of a maritime accident - the response to the criminalisation of seafarers - and the joint database on abandonment of seafarers, which sits alongside the MLC's financial-security requirement.
ILO Convention No. 185, Seafarers' Identity Documents, 2003, supports shore leave and transit, and is the labour-side counterpart to the FAL Convention's facilitation provisions.

The state of the MLC at this sitting must be stated in two parts. The 2022 amendments are in force, from 23 December 2024, and are integrated above. A further set of amendments was adopted on 6 June 2025 at the 113th Session of the International Labour Conference - three months before this examination - and was NOT in force, entry into force being expected in December 2027 under the Convention's tacit-acceptance mechanism. They comprise seven themed items touching Regulations 1.4, 2.4, 2.5, 3.1, 4.1, 4.3, 4.4 and 5.1: repatriation without discrimination; a new Standard A2.4.2 on shore leave; recognition of seafarers as key workers; fair treatment and marine casualties; the costs of repatriation the shipowner must bear; medical training; and violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, bullying and sexual assault. Naming them as adopted and awaiting entry into force is the correct answer at this sitting - they were neither absent from the regime nor yet part of the operative law.

blocks.h: 7. B) The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The guidance is MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', of 24 January 2019, approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee and finalized by the HTW Sub-Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - the binding rest-hour requirements remain in STCW chapter VIII and in MLC 2006. The Guidelines are arranged in six modules, each addressed to a different party:

ul: Module 1 - Fatigue: what it is and its causes, grouped as sleep and rest, the biological clock and circadian rhythm, health and stress, environmental factors such as noise, vibration and motion, sleep disorders and operational factors. It defines sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods.
Module 2 - Fatigue and the Company: assessing, mitigating and managing fatigue risk within the safety management system, in manning decisions and in scheduling.

Module 3 - Fatigue and the Seafarer: practical guidance for the master, officers and ratings on sleep quality, diet and the limits of countermeasures - notably that caffeine is not a substitute for sleep.
Module 4 - Fatigue Awareness and Training.
Module 5 - Fatigue and Ship Design: mitigation designed in - accommodation location, noise, vibration, lighting and habitability.
Module 6 - Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities: how regulators and inspectors should approach it.

blocks.h: 8. How the guidance and the mandatory rules fit together

blocks.p: The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are set by a prescriptive formula. Under the Manila-amended section A-VIII/1 the minimum is 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period; the daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive rest periods shall not exceed 14 hours. Authorised exceptions may not take weekly rest below 70 hours, may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and permit division into no more than three periods. MLC Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7 run the same way from the labour side.

The management-level point, and the one that separates a Class I answer from a recitation of numbers, is that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested. The Guidelines require managers to allow for circadian rhythm and accumulated sleep debt, and are explicit that rest means rest, not the substitution of a different form of work. A management-level engineer should therefore treat recorded compliance as the floor, and a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant as a warning rather than a reassurance - because the record is generated by the very person whose hours it records, under commercial pressure, on a ship manned to the minimum.

The paper prints no mark allocation for this question, so treat it as an even split and give each limb equal weight. The commonest way to lose limb (a) is to answer it as a second STCW question. The stem says IMO, ILO regimes and then names maritime labour and welfare - that is a signpost to MLC 2006, and an answer that never reaches the MLC has missed the centre of the limb. The safe structure is IMO side, ILO side, then where they meet, because it lets you show the architecture rather than list instruments.

blocks.h: The one sentence that organises the whole of limb (a)

blocks.p: IMO regulates the seafarer as the operator of a ship; ILO regulates the seafarer as a worker. Everything else hangs off that. It also explains the overlap that examiners like to probe: hours of rest appear in both regimes, in STCW section A-VIII/1 and in MLC Standard A2.3, because the seafarer's terms of employment and the safety of the ship are the same question asked twice. If you can state the division and then name the overlap, you have the analytical mark before you list anything.

blocks.h: Adopted, in force, and why September 2025 sits between two sets of amendments

blocks.p: This is the trap on this question and it runs in both directions.

ul: The 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024, nine months before this sitting. They are not a recent development to be mentioned in passing - they are the law, and the right way to use them is to state their requirements in the Title they amend: social connectivity under Title 3, appropriately-sized PPE and the precedence of controls over PPE under Title 4, and the reporting of deaths to the ILO global register as a flag-State duty.

The 2025 amendments were adopted on 6 June 2025, three months before this sitting, and were not in force. Both errors are available here. Leaving them out altogether is wrong, because they had been adopted before you sat the paper and a question about the regimes is a question about the state of the regime. Treating them as operative requirements is equally wrong. The correct answer names them and marks them as awaiting entry into force.

Note the asymmetry with a question that asks for the provisions and requirements of the MLC. There, the 2025 set has no place at all, because it imposes no requirement yet. The wording of the stem decides it.

blocks.p: Worth knowing in outline, because it is the direction of travel and makes a strong closing paragraph. Seven themed items: repatriation without discrimination and irrespective of flag; a new Standard A2.4.2 on shore leave, including that no seafarer shall be required to hold a visa or special permit for shore leave; designation of seafarers as key workers with safe movement for crew changes and medical care ashore; fair treatment, requiring account to be taken of the Casualty Investigation Code and the ILO/IMO fair-treatment guidelines in casualty inquiries; the costs of repatriation the shipowner must bear, itemised as passage, accommodation and food, up to 30 kg of personal luggage and necessary medical treatment; updated medical training references; and a substantial package on violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, bullying and sexual assault, with reference to the Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190), requiring shipowner policies, definitions, reporting mechanisms and confidentiality safeguards.

A warning about secondary sources on this point. Summaries in wide circulation state that the amendments touch Regulations 1.4, 2.1, 2.4, 2.5, 4.3, 4.4 and 5.1. That list is wrong. Regulation 2.1 is not amended, and Regulations 3.1 and 4.1 are. The number seven counts the themed items, not the Regulations. This was found by reading the ILO instrument rather than the summaries.

"The IMO guidance" is a specific document, and naming it - MSC.1/Circ.1598 of 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001 - together with its six modules is most of the limb. Candidates who write generally about tiredness score very little. The second half of the limb is the relationship between recommendatory guidance and mandatory formula, and that is where the management-level marks are.

blocks.h: The wrong-edition hazard on the rest-hour figures

blocks.p: A freely available IMO STCW.6/Circ.1 copy of section A-VIII/1 gives a five-paragraph pre-Manila text: 70 hours of rest in each seven-day period, and no 14-hour interval provision at all. That is the 1995 Code. A candidate revising from it writes 70 where 77 is required and omits the 14-hour rule entirely. The document is official, on an official domain, and superseded. The lesson generalises: ask which edition, not whether it is official.

ul: Answering limb (a) as an STCW question and never reaching MLC 2006, when the stem names maritime labour and welfare.
Describing the MLC as having four Titles. It has five; Title 5 is compliance and enforcement and is what makes the rest enforceable.
Quoting a ratification count. Any figure you have read is almost certainly current rather than as at this sitting, and the question does not need one.

Confusing the two rest regimes. STCW A-VIII/1 sets a minimum rest standard; MLC Standard A2.3.5 lets the Member fix either maximum hours of work (14/72) or minimum hours of rest (10/77). Writing 14/72 as though it were the rest standard is a common slip.
Treating the 2025 amendments as operative, or omitting them entirely. Both are temporal errors at this sitting.
Filling limb (a) with fatigue material. Fatigue belongs in limb (a) only as fitness for duty; if it fills limb (a), limb B) has nothing left to say.

Is connectivity a legal requirement? Yes. Standard A3.1 paragraph 17 requires recreational facilities including social connectivity, with guidance on internet access at reasonable charges. It is not a commercial courtesy.

Does the MLC require PPE, or something more? More. Standard A4.3 paragraph 1(b) requires appropriately-sized PPE, and Guideline B4.3.1 paragraph 3 with Standard A4.3 paragraph 2 requires that control and substitution take precedence over PPE - the hierarchy of controls, express in the Convention.
Who draws each part of the DMLC? Part I the competent authority, listing national requirements; Part II the shipowner, setting out the measures for ongoing compliance. Reversing them is a giveaway.
Why does a non-ratifying flag not escape? Article V.7 - no more favourable treatment.

Is MSC.1/Circ.1598 mandatory? No. Its force comes from the mandatory instruments it sits beside, and from the ISM Code, under which a company that ignores known fatigue risk has a defective safety management system.
Which four instruments are the pillars of maritime regulation? SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and MLC 2006.
How is the MLC Code divided, and which half is mandatory? Part A Standards, mandatory; Part B Guidelines, due consideration.
What is substantial equivalence, and where is it? Article VI.3.
Give the minimum hours of rest under STCW. 10 in any 24, 77 in any 7 days, no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, interval not exceeding 14 hours.
Name the IMO fatigue guidance and one of its modules. MSC.1/Circ.1598; for example Module 5, Fatigue and Ship Design.
What triggers a detailed MLC port State inspection? Any of the four in Standard A5.2.1.1.
Name the IMO resolution on the human element. A.947(23).

blocks.p: Limb (a): OPERATOR then WORKER then TOGETHER. Under OPERATOR, S-I-M - STCW, ISM, Manning. Under WORKER, the five Titles as W-H-A-H-E: Who may sail (1), How they are employed (2), Accommodation and food (3), Health and welfare (4), Enforcement (5). Under TOGETHER, F-A-I-R - Fair treatment guidelines, Abandonment database, Identity documents (C185), and what Remains to come into force. Limb B): 1598, six modules, floor not ceiling.

questions.understand_first: The human element is regulated twice over, by two organisations, for two different reasons. IMO is interested in the seafarer because an unsafe or incompetent operator endangers the ship; ILO is interested in the seafarer because a seafarer is a worker with rights. That is why STCW asks whether you are competent and fit for duty, while the MLC asks what you are paid, where you sleep and when you go home. The two regimes are not alternatives and they are not duplicates - they meet at hours of rest, which is simultaneously a condition of employment and a condition of safety, and that overlap is the single most examinable idea in the topic.

retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 what the human element is and how IMO and ILO divide the work. 2 the IMO regime - STCW, ISM, safe manning. 3 the ILO regime - MLC 2006 architecture. 4 what the maritime labour and welfare regime requires. 5 Title 5 enforcement. 6 where the two act jointly, and the status of the amendments at this sitting. retrieval_cards.prompt: In one sentence, how do the IMO and ILO regimes on the human element differ, and where do they meet?
retrieval_cards.answer: IMO regulates the seafarer as the operator of a ship - competence, watchkeeping, fitness for duty and safe operation; ILO regulates the seafarer as a worker - employment, wages, hours, accommodation, welfare and social protection. They meet at hours of rest, which appears in both STCW section A-VIII/1 and MLC Standard A2.3, because a seafarer's terms of employment and the safety of the ship are the same question asked twice.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the analytical mark on limb (a). Everything else in the limb is a list that hangs off this sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: At September 2025, what was the status of the two most recent sets of MLC amendments?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2022 amendments were IN FORCE, from 23 December 2024, nine months before the sitting - they are simply the law and belong integrated into the Titles they amend. The 2025 amendments were ADOPTED on 6 June 2025 at the 113th Session of the International Labour Conference, three months before the sitting, but were NOT in force, entry into force being expected in December 2027.
retrieval_cards.why: The trap runs both ways. Omitting the 2025 set is an error because it was adopted before the paper was sat; applying it as operative is the opposite error. Adopted is not in force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the MLC 2006 built, and which parts bind?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three parts - the Articles, the Regulations and the Code. Article VI divides the Code: Part A contains Standards and is mandatory; Part B contains Guidelines, which are not mandatory but to which Members must give due consideration. Article VI.3 permits substantial equivalence. Article IV states the underlying rights. The Regulations and Code are arranged in five Titles, the fifth being compliance and enforcement.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming five Titles and the Part A / Part B split is the fastest way to show you know the instrument rather than its reputation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the two rest-hour regimes and keep them apart.
retrieval_cards.answer: STCW section A-VIII/1 sets minimum rest: 10 hours in any 24 and 77 hours in any 7 days, divided into no more than two periods one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rests. MLC Standard A2.3.5 requires the Member to fix EITHER maximum hours of work - 14 in any 24 and 72 in any 7 days - OR minimum hours of rest - 10 in any 24 and 77 in any 7 days.
retrieval_cards.why: Writing 14/72 as though it were the rest standard is the commonest numerical slip in this topic. The MLC offers an election; STCW does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the IMO fatigue guidance, its date, what it replaced, and its force.
retrieval_cards.answer: MSC.1/Circ.1598, Guidelines on fatigue, of 24 January 2019, approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee and finalized by the HTW Sub-Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - the binding rest-hour requirements remain in STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'the IMO guidance', which is a specific document. Naming it and its predecessor is most of the limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the six modules of MSC.1/Circ.1598.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Fatigue - what it is and its causes, defining sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods. 2 Fatigue and the Company. 3 Fatigue and the Seafarer. 4 Fatigue Awareness and Training. 5 Fatigue and Ship Design. 6 Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities.
retrieval_cards.why: Each module is addressed to a different party, which is the structural point: fatigue is not treated as the individual's problem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant a warning rather than a reassurance?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the record is generated by the person whose hours it records, under commercial pressure, on a ship manned to the minimum. The Guidelines are explicit that complying with the prescriptive formula is not the same as being rested - circadian rhythm and accumulated sleep debt determine the quality of rest - and that rest means rest, not the substitution of a different form of work.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level judgement that separates a Class I answer from a recitation of numbers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is MLC compliance certified and enforced in a foreign port?
retrieval_cards.answer: The flag State, or an authorized recognized organization, issues a maritime labour certificate for not more than five years with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversaries. It carries the DMLC - Part I by the competent authority, Part II by the shipowner. In a foreign port the certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence; Standard A5.2.1.1 gives four triggers for a detailed inspection, and detention follows where conditions are clearly hazardous or the breach serious or repeated.
retrieval_cards.why: Title 5 is what makes the labour regime enforceable rather than aspirational, and it is the part candidates most often omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name three requirements the 2022 amendments added, and say where each belongs.
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A3.1 paragraph 17 - recreational facilities including social connectivity, with guidance on internet access at reasonable charges, in Title 3. Standard A4.3 paragraph 1(b) - appropriately-sized personal protective equipment, with Guideline B4.3.1 paragraph 3 requiring that control and substitution take precedence over PPE, in Title 4. Standard A4.3 paragraph 5(a) - all deaths investigated, recorded and reported annually to the Director-General of the ILO for a global register, also Title 4.
retrieval_cards.why: They are in force at this sitting, so they must be stated as requirements inside their Titles, not appended as a paragraph about amendments.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do the 2025 amendments cover, and which Regulations do they actually touch?
retrieval_cards.answer: Seven themed items: repatriation without discrimination; a new Standard A2.4.2 on shore leave, including that no seafarer shall be required to hold a visa for shore leave; designation of seafarers as key workers; fair treatment of seafarers and marine casualties; the costs of repatriation the shipowner must bear; medical training; and violence and harassment including sexual harassment, bullying and sexual assault. They touch Regulations 1.4, 2.4, 2.5, 3.1, 4.1, 4.3, 4.4 and 5.1.
retrieval_cards.why: Widely circulated summaries give the list as 1.4, 2.1, 2.4, 2.5, 4.3, 4.4 and 5.1, which is wrong - Regulation 2.1 is not amended and Regulations 3.1 and 4.1 are. Seven counts the themed items, not the Regulations.

retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.947(23), Human Element Vision, Principles and Goals, adopted 27 November 2003, which sets vision and principles rather than requirements. The ISM Code, at elements 6 resources and personnel, 8 emergency preparedness and drills, and 9 reports and analysis of non-conformities and accidents. blocks.h: 1. What a classification society is, and its two distinct roles

blocks.p: A classification society is a technical body that publishes its own rules for the design, construction and survey of ships, assigns class to a ship that meets them, and maintains that class by periodical survey. Its origin is commercial: underwriters needed an independent judgement of the ship they were asked to insure. Everything else follows from that.
The distinction that must be made at the outset is that a society wears two hats:

ul: Classification - a private, contractual relationship with the owner, under the society's own rules. Class is not a government function, and the society does not act for the flag State when it assigns it.

Statutory work as a Recognized Organization - work delegated by the flag State under SOLAS regulation XI-1/1, in which the society surveys and certifies against the conventions on the Administration's behalf and subject to the Code for Recognized Organizations, resolutions MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory since 1 January 2015. Here the society acts for the flag State, which retains responsibility.

blocks.p: Rules are not written from theory alone. They are built from service experience - damage and defect returns from the surveyed fleet; from casualty investigation; from research and direct calculation, including finite element analysis and fatigue assessment; and from technical committees drawing on owners, builders, makers and the society's own surveyors. Because a ship trades worldwide and changes flag and society, divergence between societies is itself a hazard, so the members harmonise through IACS: Unified Requirements setting minimum standards each member must implement, Unified Interpretations of convention text, Procedural Requirements, and jointly developed rules - most importantly the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers.

blocks.h: 3. What the structural, mechanical and electrical rules cover

ul: Structural - scantlings of plating, stiffeners and primary members; longitudinal and local strength; fatigue life; corrosion additions and coating requirements; loading conditions and hull girder limits; and the enhanced close-up survey requirements for bulk carriers and tankers.

Mechanical - main propulsion and essential auxiliary machinery; shafting, propellers and gearing; boilers and pressure vessels; piping systems; steering gear; and the type approval of components and materials.

Electrical - generation, distribution and protection, including discrimination and short-circuit capability; essential and emergency services and their sources; cable installation; high-voltage systems; and equipment for hazardous areas.

Design - plan approval of structure, machinery and electrical installations against the rules, review of direct calculations, and type approval of equipment so that approved components need not be re-justified on each ship.

Construction - approval of materials and their manufacturers; certification of components; qualification of welding procedures and welders; witnessing of non-destructive testing and tank testing; survey during construction at the yard; and attendance at trials before the certificate is issued.

Maintenance in service - the periodical survey cycle that keeps class alive: annual, intermediate and renewal or special surveys, docking and in-water surveys, tailshaft and boiler surveys. Alternatives exist where they can be justified - continuous survey of hull or machinery spreading the items across the cycle, and an approved planned maintenance scheme allowing certain machinery items to be credited on the Chief Engineer's records. Where a defect is found, the society may impose a condition of class or recommendation with a date for rectification, and class may be suspended or withdrawn if it is not met.

blocks.h: 5. Why compliance with class rules is now mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1

blocks.p: The reference is SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1, "Structural, mechanical and electrical requirements for ships". It provides that ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society which is recognized by the Administration in accordance with the provisions of regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration which provide an equivalent level of safety.

The reason it is there is the gap it closes. SOLAS regulates subdivision and damage stability, machinery and electrical installations, fire protection and life-saving. But SOLAS never contained scantling rules - it does not state how thick a plate must be or what section modulus a hull girder must have. That had always been left to the classification societies as a matter of private contract between owner, society and underwriter. The consequence was that, as a matter of convention law, there was no requirement that a ship be built to any structural standard at all: class was commercially indispensable and legally optional.
Regulation II-1/3-1 converts that commercial arrangement into a statutory obligation, and four things follow:

ul: compliance with a recognized society's rules becomes a SOLAS requirement, enforceable by the flag State and inspectable by port State control;
the obligation runs to maintenance, not only to design and construction - so loss or suspension of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance, not merely a commercial and insurance problem;
the society whose rules are relied on must be recognized under XI-1/1 and must operate under the RO Code, so the standard is not simply whatever any body chooses to publish; and
an Administration may still use its own national standards, but only where they provide an equivalent level of safety - preserving flag State sovereignty without opening a loophole.

blocks.p: This also completes the picture begun by goal-based standards: for bulk carriers and oil tankers, the class rules relied on under II-1/3-1 must themselves have been verified at IMO as conforming to the goals and functional requirements under SOLAS II-1/3-10. SOLAS therefore requires compliance with class rules, and separately requires those rules to have been shown to be good enough.
(The printed question refers to "SOLAS ch.ll-1", using two lowercase letter L's. The reference intended is chapter II-1, and within it regulation 3-1.)

blocks.h: 6. The harmonized system, and where these surveys sit

blocks.p: Before harmonization, each certificate carried its own survey dates, so a ship could be under survey almost continuously and a certificate could expire while the ship was at sea. The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and extended to MARPOL, aligns the certificates on a common five-year cycle with common anniversary dates and a common window of three months either side, so that surveys can be taken together. The guidance in force is the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2023, resolution A.1186(33), adopted 6 December 2023, which revokes A.1156(32). The system uses initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal and additional surveys, plus inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom.

blocks.p: The relevance is that a five-year certificate would otherwise be an unverified assertion. The renewal survey establishes the ship's condition at the start of the cycle; the annual and periodical surveys are the checkpoints that keep that finding credible through it, and their common window is what allows them to be combined into a single attendance rather than surveying the ship piecemeal. The periodical survey exists because life-saving, fire-fighting and radio equipment deteriorates and is consumed in a way structure does not - so equipment gets a searching mid-cycle test, and the radio installation, on which distress communication depends absolutely, gets one every year.

The printed split is 10 + 6, the only unequal split on this paper, and it must be respected. Limb (a) carries three tasks in ten marks - rule formation, implementation across the lifecycle, and the SOLAS reason - and the third of those is where the discrimination lies, so it deserves real space rather than a closing sentence. Limb (b) is six marks for a comparison: a table earns them faster than prose, and there is no credit for padding it out.

blocks.h: The heart of limb (a): what gap does II-1/3-1 close?

blocks.p: Most candidates will state that SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires compliance with class rules. Very few will say why that regulation had to exist, and that is the whole question. SOLAS has never contained scantling rules - it does not say how thick a plate must be. Structural standards were always a matter of private contract between owner, society and underwriter. So before II-1/3-1, a ship could in principle satisfy SOLAS while being built to no structural standard whatever, because class was commercially indispensable but legally optional. The regulation makes it legally compulsory, and extends the duty to maintenance - which is what turns loss of class from a commercial problem into a convention breach that port State control can act on.

blocks.h: The two-hats distinction is the other half of limb (a)

blocks.p: Classification is private and contractual; statutory certification as a Recognized Organization is delegated by the flag State under SOLAS XI-1/1 and governed by the RO Code. The same surveyor may do both on the same day, which is exactly why the distinction is worth stating. Note the resolution numbers carefully: the RO Code is MSC.349(92) with MEPC.237(65), mandatory from 1 January 2015. Getting the session number wrong here is an easy and visible slip.

blocks.h: Limb (b) has one fact almost nobody knows

blocks.p: The periodical survey is not simply "the survey that happens periodically". It attaches to only two certificates - Safety Equipment and Safety Radio - and it has a different frequency for each. For the Safety Equipment Certificate it falls at the second or third anniversary and replaces one of the annual surveys. For the Safety Radio Certificate it falls at every anniversary. A candidate who states both frequencies and notes that the radio survey is annual because distress communication cannot be allowed to degrade unnoticed has said something precise where most answers say something vague.

blocks.h: Why harmonization was needed at all

blocks.p: The point of HSSC is not the survey types; it is the alignment. Before it, certificates carried independent dates, so a ship might be under survey almost continuously and could still find a certificate expiring at sea. HSSC puts everything on a common five-year cycle with common anniversary dates and a common three-months-either-side window, so surveys can be combined into one attendance. If limb (b) explains the alignment rather than merely listing survey names, it has answered "relevance" as well as "difference".

blocks.h: Which edition of the Survey Guidelines - and why the answer here is NOT the one you will find today

blocks.p: The Survey Guidelines under the HSSC are re-adopted by the IMO Assembly roughly every two years, and each edition revokes the last. At the date of this examination the operative edition was resolution A.1186(33), the 2023 Guidelines, adopted 6 December 2023 and revoking A.1156(32).

Be careful with anything you read about this now. The 34th Assembly session adopted A.1207(34), the 2025 Guidelines, on 3 December 2025 - three months after this paper was sat. Current material will tell you that A.1186(33) has been revoked and that citing it is a mistake. For this sitting that is exactly backwards. The substance is unaffected either way: the annual and periodical survey definitions, frequencies and certificate attachments are the same in both editions. Only the resolution number and date differ - which is what makes this the most dangerous kind of error, because an answer citing the wrong edition reads as entirely correct.

ul: Treating classification and statutory certification as the same activity. One is private contract; the other is delegated flag State authority.
Saying SOLAS contains the structural rules. It does not - that is precisely why II-1/3-1 refers out to class rules.
Citing the RO Code as MSC.349(90). It is MSC.349(92), with MEPC.237(65).
Saying periodical surveys apply to all certificates. They apply only to the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificates.
Giving one frequency for the periodical survey. There are two, depending on the certificate.
Confusing the periodical survey with the intermediate survey. Both may fall at the second or third anniversary, but the intermediate attaches to different certificates and has a different scope.
Citing A.1207(34) as the Survey Guidelines for this sitting. That resolution was adopted on 3 December 2025, after this examination. The edition in force here is A.1186(33).
Forgetting that II-1/3-1 permits national standards of equivalent safety as an alternative to class rules.

blocks.p:
"Your ship loses class mid-voyage. Is that a SOLAS matter?" Yes. II-1/3-1 requires the ship to be maintained in compliance with the rules of a recognized society, so loss of class is a convention non-compliance and not merely a commercial and insurance issue.

"Must a ship be classed?" Strictly, it must comply with the requirements of a recognized society or with national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety. In practice class is universal, but the regulation offers the alternative and saying so shows the text has been read.

"When is your periodical survey due?" Ask which certificate. Safety Equipment: second or third anniversary, in place of an annual. Safety Radio: every anniversary.

"Who is responsible if the recognized organization gets it wrong?" The Administration. Recognition delegates the work, not the responsibility - which is the point of the RO Code.

ul: Which SOLAS regulation requires compliance with class rules, and where does the recognition come from? II-1/3-1, with recognition under XI-1/1.
What is the RO Code and when did it become mandatory? MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory from 1 January 2015.
Name three IACS instrument types. Unified Requirements, Unified Interpretations, Procedural Requirements.
What is the harmonized survey window? Three months before or after the anniversary date.
Which certificates carry a periodical survey? Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio.
Which resolution carried the HSSC Survey Guidelines at this sitting? A.1186(33), adopted 6 December 2023, revoking A.1156(32).
What is a condition of class? A defect the society requires to be rectified by a stated date, failing which class may be suspended or withdrawn.
What alternatives to open survey exist for machinery? Continuous survey of machinery, and an approved planned maintenance scheme.

blocks.p: For limb (a), three lifecycle verbs: approve, witness, survey - plan approval at design, witnessing at construction, periodical survey in service (step 4). For the SOLAS reason, one sentence: SOLAS never had scantlings, so it borrowed class's (step 5). For limb (b), annual is a look, periodical is a test - and periodical belongs to only two certificates (step 7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Two hats. Classification is a private, contractual relationship with the owner under the society's own rules - not a government function. Statutory work as a Recognized Organization is delegated by the flag State under SOLAS XI-1/1, governed by the RO Code, MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory since 1 January 2015; the Administration retains responsibility. Rules are made from service experience and defect returns, casualty investigation, research and direct calculation including FEA and fatigue assessment, and technical committees - harmonised across societies through IACS: Unified Requirements, Unified Interpretations, Procedural Requirements, and the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers. They cover structural (scantlings, hull girder strength, fatigue, corrosion additions, close-up survey), mechanical (propulsion, shafting, boilers, piping, steering gear, type approval) and electrical (generation, distribution and protection, essential and emergency services, high voltage, hazardous areas). Implementation: plan approval and type approval at design; material and welder qualification, NDT and tank testing witnessed, survey during construction and trials; in service the survey cycle, with continuous survey and an approved planned maintenance scheme as alternatives, and a condition of class where a defect is found - class may be suspended or withdrawn. Why it is in SOLAS: regulation II-1/3-1 requires ships to be designed, constructed AND maintained to the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a society recognized under XI-1/1, or to national standards of equivalent safety. It exists because SOLAS never contained scantling rules - structural standards were private contract, so class was commercially indispensable but legally optional. Now compliance is a convention requirement, it runs to maintenance so loss of class is a SOLAS non-compliance inspectable by port State control, and under II-1/3-10 the rules relied on must themselves be verified as conforming to goal-based standards. (b) HSSC, from the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols, aligns certificates on a common five-year cycle, common anniversary dates and a common three months either side window so surveys combine into one attendance. Guidelines at this sitting: A.1186(33), HSSC 2023, adopted 6 December 2023, revoking A.1156(32). Annual survey - Safety Equipment, Safety Construction and Load Line certificates; every anniversary, three months either side; a certificate examination and visual examination with certain tests, confirming maintenance and no unapproved modifications. Periodical survey - ONLY Safety Equipment and Safety Radio; Equipment at the second or third anniversary in place of an annual, Radio at EVERY anniversary; an inspection with tests when necessary of the equipment plus a documentation check. Relevance: a five-year certificate would otherwise be an unverified assertion - the renewal survey sets the condition, the annual and periodical surveys keep it credible, and equipment is tested harder because it is consumed in a way structure is not.

questions.understand_first: The odd thing about SOLAS is what it does not contain. It has a great deal to say about stability, fire and life-saving, and nothing at all about how thick a plate has to be. Hull strength was always the classification societies' private business with the owner and the underwriter. Regulation II-1/3-1 is SOLAS pointing at that private rule book and saying: that one, and you must keep to it for the ship's whole life - which is how losing class stopped being a commercial embarrassment and became a breach of the Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the classification societies and surveys question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a class society is and its two roles. 2 How rules are made. 3 What the rules cover. 4 Implementation through the ship's life. 5 Why compliance is now in SOLAS II-1. 6 The harmonized system. 7 Annual versus periodical.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 5 are the ten-mark limb (a); steps 6 and 7 are the six-mark limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the two roles a classification society performs.
retrieval_cards.answer: Classification is a private, contractual relationship with the owner under the society's own rules. Statutory certification as a Recognized Organization is work delegated by the flag State under SOLAS XI-1/1, governed by the RO Code, in which the society acts for the Administration - which retains responsibility.
retrieval_cards.why: The same surveyor may do both on the same day, which is exactly why the distinction has to be stated.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 require?
retrieval_cards.answer: That ships be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society recognized by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety.
retrieval_cards.why: Note all three verbs - designed, constructed AND maintained. The third is what makes loss of class a convention breach.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did SOLAS need regulation II-1/3-1 at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because SOLAS never contained scantling rules. Structural standards were a matter of private contract between owner, society and underwriter, so class was commercially indispensable but legally optional. II-1/3-1 makes compliance a convention requirement, extending to maintenance.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating point of the whole question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the RO Code and when did it become mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Code for Recognized Organizations, adopted by resolutions MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory from 1 January 2015 under SOLAS, MARPOL and the Load Line Protocol.
retrieval_cards.why: It is MSC.349(92), not (90) - an easy and visible slip.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When is an annual survey due, and what is its scope?
retrieval_cards.answer: Within three months before or after each anniversary date of the certificate. It consists of a certificate examination, a visual examination of sufficient extent of the ship and its equipment and certain tests, confirming the condition is being maintained and that no unapproved modifications have been made.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'no unapproved modifications' limb is the part most candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which certificates carry a periodical survey, and when is it due?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate and the Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate. For Safety Equipment, within three months before or after the second or third anniversary date, taking the place of one of the annual surveys. For Safety Radio, within three months before or after each anniversary date.
retrieval_cards.why: Two certificates, two different frequencies - the fact most answers miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a periodical survey differ in character from an annual survey?
retrieval_cards.answer: An annual survey is largely a visual confirmation that maintenance is being kept up. A periodical survey is an inspection with tests when necessary of the equipment itself, confirming it complies, is in satisfactory condition and is fit for the intended service, together with a documentation check.
retrieval_cards.why: Annual is a look; periodical is a test. Equipment is consumed in a way structure is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution carried the HSSC Survey Guidelines at this sitting - and why must you be careful looking this up now?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1186(33), Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023, revoking A.1156(32). Be careful because A.1207(34) was adopted on 3 December 2025 - three months AFTER this examination - and current material will tell you A.1186(33) is revoked. For this sitting it is the correct citation.
retrieval_cards.why: The survey substance is identical in both editions, so a wrong citation yields an answer that reads as entirely correct. That is what makes it dangerous.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship loses class mid-voyage. Is that only a commercial problem?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires the ship to be maintained in compliance with a recognized society's rules, so loss of class is a convention non-compliance, enforceable by the flag State and inspectable by port State control.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the practical consequence of the word 'maintained' in the regulation.
